title: Rome in One Level
objective: After this level you can describe the three big eras of Roman history and roughly when each began and ended.
summary: Rome went from Kingdom to Republic (509 BCE) to Empire (27 BCE). It ringed the Mediterranean; the West fell in 476 and the East in 1453.

cards.headline: Rome tried kings, then a Republic, then emperors. Then it fell. Twice.
cards.body: That’s the whole plot. It took more than a thousand years to play out, and even the ending was in no hurry.

mascot.line: Keep these three eras handy. Everything later in this tree hangs on one of them.

cards.headline: Kingdom, Republic, Empire
cards.body: Romans dated their city’s founding to 753 BCE, and at first it was ruled by kings: the Kingdom. In 509 BCE the Romans threw out their last king and ran things as a Republic instead. That lasted until 27 BCE, when Augustus took sole power and the Empire began. Same city, three very different answers to one question: who’s in charge here?
cards.callout: Kingdom → Republic (509 BCE) → Empire (27 BCE)

cards.headline: An empire around a sea
cards.body: At its height, Rome held every coast of the Mediterranean, stretching from Britain to Egypt and from Spain to the Middle East. Picture it on a map: a giant ring of land with a sea in the middle. So Romans simply called the Mediterranean Mare Nostrum, “our sea.” Sail anywhere on it, and wherever you landed, you were still in Rome’s empire.

cards.fact: Rome fell twice.
cards.context: The western half of the empire ended in 476 CE, when its last emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed. The eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, kept going until 1453, almost a thousand years later. So if someone asks you when Rome fell, the honest answer is another question: which half?

title: Romulus and Remus
objective: After this level you can retell Rome’s founding legend and explain why Romans valued it.
summary: Legend says twin sons of Mars, nursed by a she-wolf, founded Rome, and Romulus killed Remus. Historians treat it as legend, not history.

cards.headline: Rome’s origin story: twins, a wolf and a murder.
cards.body: Not exactly a bedtime story. Yet the wolf became a symbol of Rome itself.

cards.headline: Raised by a wolf
cards.body: In the legend, the twins Romulus and Remus were sons of the god Mars. They were abandoned as babies, and a she-wolf found them and nursed them. Rome turned that moment into its emblem: the she-wolf feeding the twins became one of the city’s best-known symbols. Most cities don’t put a wild predator in the family photo. Rome made it the cover shot.

cards.headline: A city named in blood
cards.body: The twins grew up, and their new city came between them. They quarreled over it, and Romulus killed Remus. The winner got the naming rights: the city was named Rome, after Romulus. Imagine your hometown being named after whichever sibling won the argument. Romans didn’t have to imagine it.

mascot.line: If you keep one thing here: a legend shows who Romans wanted to be, not what happened.

cards.headline: Legend, not history
cards.body: Romans had a second origin story, too. They traced their ancestry to Aeneas, a Trojan prince who, in legend, fled the fall of Troy to Italy. Historians treat both stories as legend, because they were written down centuries after the events they describe. So why learn them? Because they show how Romans saw themselves. A legend won’t tell you what happened, but it tells you who a people wanted to be.

title: What the Ground Remembers
objective: After this level you can explain what archaeology shows about Rome’s earliest villages.
summary: Latin farmers built huts on the Palatine by about the 8th century BCE. Hilltop villages merged, and the marshy Forum valley was drained.

cards.headline: Forget the wolf for a moment. What does the ground say?
cards.body: Under the ruins on Rome’s Palatine Hill lie traces of the city’s first huts. They tell a quieter story than twins and a she-wolf.

cards.headline: Huts on a hill
cards.body: The first Romans were Latins, a people of the region of Latium in central Italy. On the Palatine Hill, archaeologists have found traces of their Iron Age huts from around the 8th century BCE. Now hold that next to the traditional founding date, 753 BCE. The huts sit close to the traditional founding: the shovel and the storytellers land in the same century. Not bad for a tale with a wolf in it.

cards.headline: From villages to a town
cards.body: Early Rome wasn’t one city. It was a cluster of small hilltop villages that gradually merged into one community. Down between the hills lay a marshy valley. It was drained, and that soggy low ground became the Roman Forum, the center of Roman public life. Before it was famous, it was a bog.

cards.fact: Rome’s great drain still works.
cards.context: The Cloaca Maxima, Rome’s great drain, helped dry out that marshy Forum valley. Parts of it still carry water today. Somewhere under the modern city, a very old drain is still doing its job.

title: Seven Hills and a River
objective: After this level you can explain how the Tiber and the seven hills shaped where and why Rome grew.
summary: Rome grew at a crossing of the Tiber on a trade route, on hills that were easy to defend and stayed dry. Ostia became its port.

cards.headline: Why build a city right here? Follow the river and the salt.
cards.body: Rome sits where it does for reasons you can still see on a map: a river you can cross, a road for salt, and hills that keep your feet dry.

cards.headline: A river crossing
cards.body: Rome grew where the Tiber River could be crossed, near an island in the river, about 25 km from the sea. An ancient salt route, later called the Via Salaria, passed right through, linking the coast with inland Italy. So anyone moving goods between the two came this way. Own the crossing, and trade has to walk past your front door.
cards.callout: River crossing + trade route = a place worth holding

cards.headline: Seven hills
cards.body: The city spread across seven hills beside the Tiber, among them the Capitoline and the Palatine, where those first huts stood. The hills made sense twice over. They were easier to defend, and they stayed dry when the Tiber flooded the low ground between them. Enemies and floods: the hills handled both.

cards.fact: Rome had its own port.
cards.context: Rome sat about 25 km inland, so its harbor was downstream. Ostia, at the mouth of the Tiber, became Rome’s port. Grain and other goods came in there and traveled up the river to the city. The same river that gave Rome its crossing also delivered dinner.

title: The Etruscans Next Door
objective: After this level you can describe who the Etruscans were and what Rome borrowed from them.
summary: The Etruscans of Tuscany were early Italy’s great power. Rome had Etruscan kings and borrowed the fasces and haruspicy from them.

cards.headline: Before Rome was a great power, it lived next to one.
cards.body: The Etruscans were among the most powerful peoples of early Italy. Rome borrowed a lot from them, even, tradition says, some of its kings.

cards.headline: Rome’s powerful neighbors
cards.body: North of Rome, in Etruria, mostly what is now Tuscany, lived the Etruscans. They weren’t one kingdom but a set of independent cities, and they were among the most powerful peoples of early Italy. Their language was unrelated to Latin, and it is still only partly understood. Rome’s big neighbors next door, and we still can’t fully read their mail.

cards.headline: Etruscan kings
cards.body: Here’s the twist. According to Roman tradition, the last three kings of Rome were Etruscans. Historians can’t vouch for every detail, but the bigger picture holds: young Rome grew up under strong Etruscan influence. For a while, the neighbors weren’t just next door. They were on the throne.

cards.headline: What Rome borrowed
cards.body: Some of Rome’s most Roman-looking things were imports. Take the fasces, a bundle of rods around an axe. Attendants carried it in front of officials as a sign of their authority, and it came from the Etruscans. So did haruspicy: reading omens in the organs of sacrificed animals. A way to show power and a way to read the gods, both borrowed from next door.

title: The Seven Kings
objective: After this level you can outline Rome’s age of kings and how kingship worked there.
summary: Seven kings ruled from 753 to 509 BCE, each chosen with the Senate’s and people’s approval. Numa founded religion; Servius, the census.

cards.headline: Rome had seven kings, if you trust the legends. Not the kind you picture.
cards.body: No crown passed neatly from father to son. Most of the time, Rome had other ideas about who got the job.

cards.headline: Seven kings
cards.body: Roman tradition counted seven kings, from Romulus in 753 BCE to Tarquin the Proud in 509 BCE, the last three of them Etruscans. But this wasn’t a family business. Kingship was not simply inherited: tradition says most kings were chosen with the approval of the Senate and the people. Being the old king’s son didn’t get you the job. Getting approved did.

cards.headline: Remembered for different things
cards.body: Each king came with a reputation, like a line on a résumé. Numa Pompilius, the second king, was remembered as the founder of Rome’s religious institutions and its calendar. Servius Tullius, the sixth, was credited with the first census, which sorted citizens by wealth. Ask a Roman who started a custom, and there was often a king ready to take the credit.

cards.fact: The Senate started as the king’s advisers.
cards.context: It began as a council of elders who advised the king. Keep an eye on it. The kings would go, but the Senate would stay, long after the last king was gone.

title: Gods of the Household and the State
objective: After this level you can describe early Roman religion, from household spirits to state priests and omens.
summary: Romans kept peace with the gods through correct ritual: household spirits at home, Jupiter on the Capitoline, Vesta’s fire and augury.

cards.headline: Romans rarely asked whether the gods existed. They asked what the gods wanted.
cards.body: Get the ritual right, and the gods stayed on your side. Get it wrong, and even a few birds could hold up the city’s business.

cards.headline: Keeping peace with the gods
cards.body: Roman religion was less about what you believed and more about doing the rituals correctly. The goal had a name: the pax deorum, peace with the gods. Think of it as a contract where the fine print really matters. It started at home. Every household honored the Lares and Penates, guardian spirits of the home and its food store, at a small shrine. Even the pantry had protection.

cards.headline: Gods of the state
cards.body: The city had its own gods to keep happy. On the Capitoline Hill stood Rome’s greatest temple, dedicated to Jupiter, king of the gods, together with Juno and Minerva. Meanwhile, the Vestal Virgins tended the sacred fire of Vesta, goddess of the hearth, day and night. That fire was never allowed to go out. Every home had its little shrine. Rome had a fire nobody was allowed to let die.

cards.fact: Birds could put Roman politics on hold.
cards.context: Before major public decisions, Romans consulted augurs, priests who read the will of the gods in the flight of birds. An unfavorable sign could delay public business. Imagine a big vote postponed because the wrong birds flew by.

title: The Roman Family
objective: After this level you can explain the power of the paterfamilias and how Roman families were organized.
summary: The paterfamilias held legal power over his descendants, even adults. The familia included the whole household, enslaved people too.

cards.headline: In Rome, a 40-year-old could still be under his father’s legal power.
cards.body: Growing up didn’t make you your own boss. Meet the paterfamilias.

cards.headline: The father’s power
cards.body: Every Roman family had a paterfamilias: its oldest living male. He held legal power over his children and grandchildren, even when they were grown adults with children of their own. In early Roman law this power, patria potestas, in theory reached as far as life and death. So if your grandfather was alive, he wasn’t just your boss. He was your dad’s boss too.

cards.headline: More than relatives
cards.body: To a Roman, familia meant more than relatives. It meant the whole household, including the enslaved people who lived and worked in it. The family reached back in time, too. Noble families kept wax masks of their ancestors and carried them in funeral processions. At a noble Roman funeral, the ancestors came along.

cards.fact: Roman names came in three parts.
cards.context: Take Gaius Julius Caesar. Gaius was his personal name, Julius his clan name, and Caesar the name of his family’s branch of that clan. Say a Roman man’s full name, and you’ve recited a small family tree.

title: The Last King
objective: After this level you can explain how Rome overthrew Tarquin the Proud and why it rejected kings.
summary: Tarquin the Proud ruled as a tyrant. After the Lucretia scandal, Brutus led the Romans to expel him in 509 BCE and swear off kings.

cards.headline: Rome’s kings ended with a crime, an uprising and an oath never to have another.
cards.body: The seventh king pushed too far. What came next left Romans with a lasting horror of one word: king.

cards.headline: A tyrant king
cards.body: The seventh king, Tarquin the Proud, was remembered as a tyrant who ruled by force and ignored the Senate, the very council that had begun as the king’s advisers. Then, according to tradition, the king’s son assaulted a noblewoman named Lucretia. That was the spark. The crime set off an uprising, and not just against one bad king, but against the monarchy itself.

cards.headline: No more kings
cards.body: According to tradition, the Romans, led by Lucius Junius Brutus, drove out their king in 509 BCE and ended the monarchy. Then Brutus had them swear never again to let anyone be king in Rome. Not just “no more Tarquin.” No more kings, ever.
cards.callout: The end of the monarchy: 509 BCE

mascot.line: Hold on to this hatred of “king.” It explains the title Augustus picks in Level 44.

cards.fact: Romans hated the word “king.”
cards.context: After the tyrant kings, the title rex, king, became so hated that even Rome’s most powerful later leaders avoided it. They could hold enormous power. They just couldn’t call it that.

title: A Republic Is Born
objective: After this level you can explain what a republic is and what SPQR stood for.
summary: After the kings, Rome became a res publica: elected magistrates with limited terms, the Senate and People of Rome, from 509 to 27 BCE.

cards.headline: Rome’s answer to tyranny was to share power, and keep it short.
cards.body: Rome had just sworn never to have another king. Now it needed a government where nobody could turn into one.

cards.headline: The public thing
cards.body: No king? Then who owns the state? Rome’s answer was res publica, Latin for “the public thing,” and the root of our word republic. Instead of a king, citizens elected officials called magistrates, and every one of them held power only for a limited term. Think of it as renting power, never owning it. The state belonged to the public, not to a king.

cards.headline: SPQR
cards.body: Romans called their state by four letters: SPQR, Senatus Populusque Romanus, “the Senate and People of Rome.” Read it again: there’s no king anywhere in the name. That arrangement lasted almost five centuries, from 509 BCE until Augustus took sole power in 27 BCE.
cards.callout: SPQR: the Senate and People of Rome

cards.fact: “The People” came with fine print.
cards.context: Only adult male citizens could vote. Women, enslaved people and foreigners had no vote at all. So when SPQR said “the People,” it meant a smaller crowd than everyone who lived in Rome.

title: Two Consuls, One Year
objective: After this level you can explain how consuls shared power and why their terms were short.
summary: Two consuls led Rome for one year each, commanded its armies and could block each other. Emergencies allowed a dictator for six months.

cards.headline: Rome’s top job came with a partner and an expiry date.
cards.body: Rome wanted a leader strong enough to run the state, but never strong enough to become a king. Its fix was simple and sneaky.

mascot.line: Keep this: two at the top, one year each. Watch which later generals break these limits.

cards.headline: Two at the top
cards.body: The Republic was led by two consuls, elected by the citizens every year. Each could block the other’s actions, so neither could rule alone. Picture a car with two steering wheels and two brake pedals: nobody goes on a joyride. And after one year, both stepped down. However good you were at the job, no one held supreme power for long.

cards.headline: Generals and calendars
cards.body: Consuls also commanded Rome’s armies in war. They were so central to Roman life that Romans didn’t count their years by number. They named each year after its two consuls. Imagine dating your birthday by who happened to be in charge that year. For a Roman, that was simply the date.

cards.fact: Emergencies came with a six-month limit.
cards.context: In a crisis, Rome could appoint a dictator with supreme power. Even that came with a timer: six months at most. Rome’s emergency brake had an expiry date too.

title: The Senate
objective: After this level you can describe who sat in the Senate and how it steered the Republic.
summary: The Senate was about 300 former magistrates, usually serving for life. It only gave advice, but that advice was almost always followed.

cards.headline: The Senate couldn’t pass laws. It ran Rome anyway.
cards.body: Consuls came and went every year. So who remembered how things were done?

cards.headline: A council of former officials
cards.body: Remember the council of elders that advised the kings back in Level 6? It outlived them. In the Republic, the Senate was made up of former magistrates, men who had already held office, and they usually stayed senators for life. For most of the Republic there were about 300 of them. The only way into the room was to have helped run Rome already.

cards.headline: Advice that was obeyed
cards.body: Formally, the Senate only gave advice to the magistrates. In practice, its advice was almost always followed, especially on foreign policy and money. Why? A consul had one year. The senators facing him had all held office before and would sit there for life. When a room like that “suggests” something, you listen.

cards.fact: The Senate met in the middle of everything.
cards.context: Its usual home was the Curia, a building in the Roman Forum, the center of Roman public life. Rome’s most powerful advisers met a short walk from the markets and law courts.

title: Patricians and Plebeians
objective: After this level you can explain the Conflict of the Orders between Rome’s old families and ordinary citizens.
summary: Plebeians won rights from the patricians over two centuries, starting with a walkout in 494 BCE and ending with the Hortensian law of 287.

cards.headline: What if the workers and soldiers of a city simply walked out?
cards.body: In Rome, they did. It was the opening move in a fight over who got a say, and it lasted about two centuries.

cards.headline: Two kinds of citizen
cards.body: Every Roman citizen was one of two kinds. Patricians belonged to Rome’s old aristocratic families. Plebeians were all the rest. In the early Republic, patricians held the priesthoods and, by tradition, the magistracies too, though some historians think a few plebeians also held early offices. Either way, the top jobs belonged mostly to one side. Rome had thrown out its king, but not its old families.

cards.headline: The walkout
cards.body: In 494 BCE, according to tradition, the plebeians tried something bold: they walked out of Rome in protest. They refused to work or fight until they won concessions. A city nobody will work or fight for is just a pile of buildings. Their long struggle for political rights, about two centuries of it, is called the Conflict of the Orders.

title: The Twelve Tables
objective: After this level you can explain why Rome wrote down its laws and what that changed.
summary: Around 450 BCE Rome wrote its laws on the Twelve Tables in the Forum, so patrician judges could no longer bend unwritten custom.

cards.headline: A law you can’t read is a law someone else controls.
cards.body: The plebeians knew it. So they demanded that Rome’s laws be written down.

cards.headline: Law in public
cards.body: Roman law used to be unwritten custom, and patrician judges could interpret it as they pleased. Imagine playing a game where only the other team knows the rules. Plebeians demanded written laws, and around 450 BCE they got them: the Twelve Tables, Rome’s first written laws, displayed in the Forum. Now anyone could check the rules, at least in principle.

cards.headline: Everyday rules
cards.body: The Twelve Tables weren’t grand speeches about liberty. They covered ordinary life: debt, property, family and damage to others. In other words, the everyday arguments neighbors actually have. Centuries later, Cicero remembered memorizing them as a boy at school, then noted that boys no longer did. Kids these days.

cards.fact: The original tablets are lost.
cards.context: They were probably destroyed when the Gauls sacked Rome. The laws survive only because later writers quoted them. So the laws written down for everyone to read are the ones nobody today can read in the original.

title: Tribunes of the Plebs
objective: After this level you can describe the tribunes’ power to protect plebeians, including the veto.
summary: Tribunes, elected by plebeians, could veto other magistrates and were sacrosanct. Ten of them protected ordinary citizens.

cards.headline: The most powerful word in Roman politics meant “I forbid.”
cards.body: The plebeians had officials of their own, and those officials could stop the powerful with a single word.

cards.headline: Protectors of the plebs
cards.body: The tribunes of the plebs were officials elected by plebeians to protect them from abuses by magistrates. Their number eventually rose to ten: ten officials whose whole job was to take the plebeians’ side. And a tribune’s door was expected to stay open day and night, so any plebeian could come and ask for help. Think of a 24-hour help desk with real political muscle behind it.

mascot.line: Don’t mix them up: consuls ran the state, and tribunes could block them for the plebs.

cards.headline: I forbid
cards.body: Remember how each consul could block the other in Level 12? A tribune could block them both. He could stop the acts of other magistrates, consuls included, simply by declaring “Veto,” Latin for “I forbid.” (A dictator was probably out of reach.) So why didn’t an angry consul just arrest him? Tribunes were sacrosanct: harming one was a religious crime. And because plebeians elected them, tribunes answered to ordinary citizens rather than to the old families.

title: Cincinnatus and the Citizen Ideal
objective: After this level you can retell the story of Cincinnatus and explain the Roman idea of civic duty.
summary: Called from his plow in 458 BCE to save Rome, Cincinnatus won and gave up power after 16 days: the model Roman citizen.

cards.headline: Rome handed a farmer supreme power. He gave it back in about 16 days.
cards.body: Remember the dictator’s six-month limit from Level 12? One man didn’t need anywhere near that.

cards.headline: Called from the plow
cards.body: In 458 BCE, according to tradition, a Roman army was trapped by its enemies. The Senate needed a rescuer, so it made Cincinnatus dictator, with supreme power. The messengers didn’t find him in a palace or a war tent. They found him plowing his farm. For the moment, the most powerful man in Rome was standing behind a plow.

cards.headline: Power returned
cards.body: Cincinnatus won the war. Then he resigned as dictator after about 16 days, far short of his six months, and went back to his farm. He gave up supreme power the moment the crisis was over. His story shows what Romans prized, the mos maiorum, “the custom of the ancestors”: duty, discipline and service to the state. Cincinnatus managed all three and still got the plowing done.

cards.fact: An American city carries his name.
cards.context: Cincinnati is named after the Society of the Cincinnati, which took its name from Cincinnatus. So a whole city is named, at one remove, after a man remembered for giving power back.

Lose to Rome, and you ended up marching for it.

title: Checkpoint: How the Republic Worked

cards.headline: Checks and balances
cards.body: It took an outsider to name the design. Polybius, a Greek historian taken to Rome as a hostage, wrote his history to explain how Rome came to dominate the Mediterranean world. Along the way he praised Rome’s government as a mix of three kinds of rule: the consuls were the monarchy, the Senate the aristocracy, and the assemblies the democracy. Each part checked the others, so none could take over. Rome kept a piece of a king, a piece of the nobles and a piece of the people, and let none of them win.

title: Carthage, Queen of the Sea
objective: After this level you can describe Carthage and why it clashed with Rome.
summary: Carthage, founded by Phoenicians in 814 BCE, ruled the western seas. In 264 BCE it and Rome went to war over Sicily: the Punic Wars.

cards.headline: Once Rome held Italy, it looked across the water and found a rival.
cards.body: By about 264 BCE Rome controlled nearly all of Italy south of the Po Valley. Across the sea waited a city that was older than Rome and far better at sea.

cards.headline: A city of traders
cards.body: Carthage began as a colony. Phoenician settlers from Tyre founded it, traditionally in 814 BCE, on the coast of what is now Tunisia. It grew rich from trade, and it guarded that trade with ships, becoming the leading naval power of the western Mediterranean. Rome was a land power with a new peninsula. Carthage was a trading house with a fleet.

cards.headline: Sicily in between
cards.body: Look at a map and the trouble is obvious. Sicily sits between Italy and North Africa, like a stepping stone in the middle of a stream. Rome now held Italy and faced Carthage, the great sea power, across the water. In 264 BCE the two went to war over control of Sicily. Romans called these wars Punic, from the Latin Punicus, “Phoenician.” The name remembers where Carthage came from.
cards.callout: Punic = Phoenician

cards.fact: Carthage was older than Rome.
cards.context: Carthage’s traditional founding date, 814 BCE, comes 61 years before Rome’s own, 753 BCE. So when the two met in Sicily, Rome was the newcomer, taking on an older city that already ruled the western sea. The upstart against the old sea power: that’s the story of the Punic Wars.

title: The First Punic War
objective: After this level you can explain how Rome built a navy and won the First Punic War.
summary: In 264–241 BCE a land power learned to fight at sea. With a new fleet and the corvus, Rome beat Carthage and took Sicily.

cards.headline: To beat a sea power, Rome had to become one, almost from scratch.
cards.body: Rome’s enemy was the leading navy of the western Mediterranean. Rome’s answer was simple and slightly outrageous: build a navy of its own.

cards.headline: A navy from nothing
cards.body: The First Punic War lasted from 264 to 241 BCE, and Rome started it with a problem. It had little experience at sea, and Carthage was the leading naval power of the western Mediterranean. So Rome built a large war fleet. Picture a team of wrestlers signing up for a swimming race against the champions. Bold. Also, on paper, a terrible idea.

cards.headline: Turning sea battles into land battles
cards.body: Rome’s trick was to change the game. Roman ships carried the corvus, a boarding bridge with a spike at its end. Drop it onto an enemy deck, and Roman soldiers could storm across and fight on enemy decks as if they were on solid ground. A sea battle became a fight between soldiers, the kind of fight Rome was good at. Can’t win the swimming race? Turn it into a wrestling match.

cards.fact: Sicily became Rome’s first province.
cards.context: Winning the war in 241 BCE gave Rome the island the fighting had started over, and with it Rome’s first overseas province. Remember that word, province. Rome was about to start collecting them.

cards.headline: A general sworn against Rome

As a Carthaginian general based in Spain, Hannibal attacked Saguntum, a Roman ally, sparking the Second Punic War, which lasted from 218 to 201 BCE. Then he invaded Italy itself, taking the war straight to Rome’s home ground.

cards.headline: Over the Alps

Oddly, most of the elephants survived the crossing, only for nearly all of them to die in the cold soon after. Still, he reached Italy and won early victories. Then he stayed. For about 15 years, Rome could not drive him out of its own backyard.

title: Disaster at Cannae
objective: After this level you can explain what happened at Cannae and why it is still studied.
summary: At Cannae in 216 BCE Hannibal encircled a much larger Roman army and destroyed it. Rome lost tens of thousands, yet refused to make peace.

cards.headline: A much larger Roman army walked into a trap it couldn’t escape.
cards.body: More soldiers usually means a better chance. At Cannae, Hannibal made Rome’s numbers work against it.

cards.headline: The trap
cards.body: At Cannae in 216 BCE, Hannibal faced a much larger Roman army. He let the center of his line fall back as the Romans pushed forward, so every step forward carried them deeper in. Then his wings and cavalry closed around them from both sides. The army doing the pushing was suddenly surrounded. This is a double envelopment: think of a hand closing into a fist, with the Romans inside.

cards.headline: A catastrophe, and a refusal

It refused to make peace. Hannibal had won a battle. He had not won the war. Officers still study Cannae as the classic example of encirclement. Rome was the first to learn that lesson, the hard way.

title: Fabius the Delayer
objective: After this level you can explain Fabius Maximus’s strategy of avoiding battle and why it worked.
summary: Fabius shadowed Hannibal and cut his supplies instead of fighting. Mocked as the Delayer, he was proved right as Italy’s allies held firm.

cards.headline: Sometimes the best way to beat a genius is to refuse to fight him.
cards.body: Hannibal kept winning battles in Italy. One Roman general’s answer sounded almost cowardly: stop giving him battles to win.

cards.headline: Don’t fight, follow
cards.body: Fabius Maximus avoided pitched battles with Hannibal. Instead he shadowed Hannibal’s army and cut off its supplies, like a shadow that also steals your lunch. Romans first used his nickname as an insult: Cunctator, “the Delayer.” After the disaster at Cannae in 216 BCE, a little delay looked a lot wiser, and the insult became praise.

mascot.line: This is Level 19’s smart move paying off: beaten peoples became allies who stayed loyal.

cards.headline: Why it worked
cards.body: Hannibal was far from home. To keep going, he needed supplies and new allies: Italian cities willing to switch sides and send him men. But Rome had bound the peoples it defeated as allies who supplied soldiers, and most of them stayed loyal. With Fabius cutting his supplies and no new allies joining, Hannibal never got the reinforcements he needed. Time was on Rome’s side.

cards.fact: His name became a strategy.
cards.context: A “Fabian strategy” still means wearing down a stronger enemy by avoiding a decisive battle, exactly as Fabius did. Not bad for a man once mocked as the Delayer.

title: The Legion
objective: After this level you can describe how a Roman legion was organized, equipped and trained.
summary: Republican legions had 4,000 to 5,000 citizen infantry in flexible maniples, three lines deep, armed with the gladius and pila.

cards.headline: Rome’s real weapon was organization.
cards.body: Cannae showed what happened when a legion got trapped. Here’s how it was built to fight.

cards.headline: Citizens under arms
cards.body: In the Republic, a legion had roughly 4,000 to 5,000 infantry: picture a small town, all on foot. In the earlier Republic, those soldiers were property-owning citizens who supplied their own equipment. War was very much bring-your-own. Each man carried a short stabbing sword, the gladius, and heavy throwing javelins called pila.

mascot.line: You don’t need all three Latin names. Remember the order: youngest in front, veterans at the back.

cards.headline: Flexible blocks
cards.body: A legion didn’t fight as one giant block. It fought in maniples, small flexible units arranged in three lines. The youngest men, the hastati, stood in front. The principes came next. The veterans, the triarii, stood at the back. So the least experienced soldiers met the enemy first, with the most experienced waiting behind them.
cards.callout: Hastati → principes → triarii

cards.fact: The pilum was hard to throw back.

title: The Gracchi Brothers
objective: After this level you can explain the land reforms of the Gracchi and why they ended in violence.
summary: As estates swallowed small farms, the tribunes Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus pushed land and grain reforms. Both were killed.

cards.headline: Two brothers tried to give land to the poor. Both were killed for it.
cards.body: Rome’s rich were getting richer while its small farmers lost their land. Two brothers tried to fix that, and found out what fixing it would cost.

cards.headline: Rich estates, poor farmers
cards.body: Picture your family farm next to a giant estate worked by enslaved people. By the 2nd century BCE, wealthy Romans had built huge estates like that, while many small farmers lost their land. In 133 BCE a tribune named Tiberius Gracchus proposed an answer: give public land to poor citizens. Remember Level 16? Tribunes of the plebs were elected to protect ordinary Romans. This one took the job literally.

cards.headline: Politics turns deadly
cards.body: The argument didn’t end with a vote. A mob of senators and their supporters killed Tiberius, the first great outbreak of political bloodshed in Rome in centuries. His brother Gaius picked up the cause and pushed even wider reforms, including cheap grain for citizens. In 121 BCE, Gaius was killed too. Two brothers, two reform plans, two funerals.

mascot.line: Keep this one. Much of the Republic’s remaining story is this lesson, learned again.

cards.fact: After the Gracchi, Roman political fights could be settled with violence.
cards.context: That was the real turning point. Not the land, but the lesson: if you couldn’t win the argument, you could get rid of the person making it. Disputes that used to be settled by votes could now be settled by violence. Watch for that lesson in the levels ahead. Rome learned it far too well.

title: Marius Remakes the Army
objective: After this level you can explain how Marius’s reforms tied soldiers to their generals.
summary: Seven-time consul Marius opened the legions to landless volunteers paid by the state. Soldiers began to look to generals, not the Senate.

cards.headline: The man who saved Rome from invaders also changed whom its soldiers served.
cards.body: Gaius Marius beat back invaders with a new kind of army. It worked brilliantly. The catch was who those soldiers answered to.

cards.headline: An army of the poor
cards.body: Remember Level 29? Legionaries used to be property-owning citizens who supplied their own gear. Gaius Marius, elected consul an unprecedented seven times, changed that. He enrolled poor citizens with no property, equipped and paid by the state. With this new army he defeated the invading Cimbri and Teutones in 102 and 101 BCE. Rome was saved. Rome was also, quietly, changed.

mascot.line: Hold on to this. Sulla and Caesar are about to show you what it means.

cards.headline: Loyal to the general
cards.body: A soldier with no property had no farm waiting for him. So who paid him, and who found him land when he retired? After Marius, soldiers increasingly looked to their general for that, not the Senate. You tend to be loyal to whoever signs your paycheck. An army loyal to its general is a useful thing, right up until the general wants something Rome doesn’t.

title: Sulla Marches on Rome
objective: After this level you can explain why Sulla’s march on Rome broke a taboo.
summary: In 88 BCE Sulla led his army against Rome itself, fought Marius’s side in a civil war, then ruled as dictator with no time limit.

cards.headline: In 88 BCE a Roman general did the unthinkable: he attacked Rome.
cards.body: Remember those soldiers who looked to their general, not the Senate? Now see what happens when a general points them at Rome.

cards.headline: The march
cards.body: In 88 BCE Sulla marched his army on Rome itself, something no Roman general had done before. His soldiers followed him, not the Senate: Marius’s reform at work, in the worst possible way. Sulla and Marius, with their supporters, then fought a civil war for control of Rome. The army that was supposed to protect the city was now fighting over it.

cards.headline: Lists of the doomed
cards.body: Sulla won, and took the dictatorship with no time limit. Remember Level 12: a dictator was meant to be an emergency ruler for six months at most. Then came the proscription lists. If your name was on one, you were an enemy who could be killed and your property seized. A public notice that was also a death warrant. Sulla reformed the constitution to strengthen the Senate, and then, surprisingly, retired.
cards.callout: Proscription: a list of enemies who could be killed

cards.headline: Why it mattered
cards.body: Sulla gave up power, but he couldn’t take back what he had shown: an army loyal to its general could be marched on Rome. Before 88 BCE, no Roman general had done it. After 88 BCE, it was no longer unthinkable, just something that had been done before. The first time is the hard part. The next general wouldn’t have to be first.

title: Spartacus
objective: After this level you can describe the slave revolt led by Spartacus and how it ended.
summary: In 73 BCE the gladiator Spartacus led a slave revolt that grew to tens of thousands. Crassus crushed it in 71 BCE.

cards.headline: A gladiator escaped his school and raised an army that shook Rome.
cards.body: It began with a breakout at a gladiator school in Capua. It ended with a road lined with crosses. In between, an army of the enslaved defeated several Roman forces.

cards.headline: The breakout
cards.body: In 73 BCE Spartacus, a gladiator from Thrace, escaped from a gladiator school at Capua and began a slave revolt. Remember those huge estates from Level 31? Their owners’ wealth depended on the enslaved people who worked them. Now those people had a leader. The rebel army grew to tens of thousands and defeated several Roman forces. The workforce had become an army.

cards.headline: A brutal end
cards.body: In 71 BCE the general Marcus Crassus crushed the revolt. Some 6,000 captured rebels were crucified along the Appian Way, the Via Appia you met in Level 19. Rome’s first great road, built to move armies, became a warning lined with crosses. Rome won the war. But Spartacus outlived his defeat, as a lasting symbol of resistance to oppression.

cards.headline: Why Rome was afraid
cards.body: Here’s why a slave army was such a nightmare for Rome’s rich. The great estates of Level 31 were worked by enslaved people, so wealthy fortunes rested on the very people now in revolt. Imagine your whole business running on workers who have walked out and started beating your security guards. That is roughly where Rome’s landowners stood.

title: Pompey the Great
objective: After this level you can describe Pompey’s rise and his conquests in the East.
summary: Pompey rose under Sulla, won huge commands, swept the pirates from the sea in 67 BCE and remade the East. He was hailed as Magnus, “the Great.”

cards.headline: His soldiers hailed him as “the Great,” and he made the name his own.
cards.body: Signing yourself “the Great” takes confidence. Pompey had it, and a string of victories to back it up. Here’s how he earned a name borrowed from Alexander.

cards.headline: A general of special commands
cards.body: Pompey first rose to fame as a young commander fighting for Sulla. Then the Roman people voted him extraordinary commands, giving one man power over huge areas for years at a time. Compare that with a consul: one year in office, and a colleague who could block him. Pompey got whole regions, for years. That’s not a job. That’s a kingdom on loan.

cards.headline: Remaking the East
cards.body: Pompey defeated King Mithridates and reorganized the eastern Mediterranean. He made Syria a Roman province and captured Jerusalem in 63 BCE. By then he already had a name to match. His troops, and Sulla too, had hailed him as Magnus, “the Great,” and Pompey used it. It echoed Alexander the Great, whom he admired and imitated. Pompey wasn’t aiming low.

cards.fact: Pompey swept the pirates from the Mediterranean in about three months.
cards.context: Three months to clear a whole sea. The campaign of 67 BCE was one of the extraordinary commands the Roman people voted him, and it shows why those commands were so powerful: one man, a huge area, and the time to finish the job.

title: Cicero Against Catiline
objective: After this level you can explain the Catiline conspiracy and Cicero’s role as consul.
summary: Cicero, a “new man” and Rome’s great orator, became consul in 63 BCE and exposed Catiline’s plot, but executed conspirators without trial.

cards.headline: Rome’s greatest speaker won his biggest fight with words, then paid for it.
cards.body: No famous family behind him, just a voice. Here’s how Cicero used it against a plot to seize Rome, and the decision that came back to bite him.

cards.headline: A new man
cards.body: Cicero was a “new man,” the first in his family to reach the Senate. Picture being the first person in your family to get into the room, and then becoming the best talker in it. His speeches made him Rome’s greatest orator. His family name opened no doors. His sentences did.

cards.headline: The conspiracy
cards.body: Cicero was elected consul for 63 BCE. That year he exposed a conspiracy by Catiline to seize power, and he denounced him in a series of famous speeches. Words won that round. Then Cicero went a step further: he had several conspirators executed without trial. Winning the argument was the easy part. Skipping the trial is what cost him. That decision later led to his exile.

cards.fact: Hundreds of Cicero’s letters survive.
cards.context: They make him the best-documented person of the late Republic. It’s a bit like reading someone’s messages two thousand years after they hit send. You get his side of the conversation, in his own words.

title: The First Triumvirate
objective: After this level you can explain the informal alliance of Caesar, Pompey and Crassus.
summary: In 60 BCE Caesar, Pompey and Crassus pooled their power. Julia’s death in 54 BCE and Crassus’s at Carrhae in 53 BCE broke it apart.

cards.headline: Three ambitious men agreed to share Rome. It couldn’t last.
cards.body: Caesar, Pompey and Crassus made a private deal to help each other get what each one wanted. Watch what held it together, and what happened when that gave way.

cards.headline: A private deal
cards.body: In 60 BCE Julius Caesar, Pompey and Crassus formed an informal alliance, later called the First Triumvirate. No law created it. It was three powerful men trading favors. Caesar got a consulship, Pompey got land for his veterans, and Crassus got favors for his allies. Everybody wins, as long as everybody stays in the deal.

cards.headline: Falling apart
cards.body: The deal had a family tie: Pompey was married to Caesar’s daughter, Julia. She died in 54 BCE, and the bond between her husband and her father weakened. Then Crassus, the man who had crushed Spartacus, was killed in 53 BCE after a disastrous defeat by the Parthians at Carrhae. A three-legged stool had lost two legs. Only two rivals were left: Caesar and Pompey.

cards.fact: Pompey married Caesar’s daughter Julia to seal the alliance.
cards.context: For a while, Rome’s great rivals were father-in-law and son-in-law. Her death in 54 BCE removed that family tie. Within a few years the two men would be fighting a civil war against each other.

title: Caesar in Gaul

summary: From 58 to 50 BCE Caesar conquered Gaul, beat Vercingetorix at Alesia, raided Britain, and gained wealth and a loyal veteran army.

cards.headline: Caesar spent eight years conquering Gaul, and wrote the history of it himself.
cards.body: Winning in Gaul made Caesar rich and gave him an army. Writing the story himself meant Rome read the war his way.

cards.headline: The conquest
cards.body: Between 58 and 50 BCE, Julius Caesar conquered Gaul. That’s eight years of campaigning. At Alesia in 52 BCE he defeated the Gallic leader Vercingetorix. Along the way he also led two expeditions across the sea to Britain, in 55 and 54 BCE. Gaul was the main event. Britain was the side quest.

cards.headline: Wealth and a loyal army
cards.body: The conquest gave Caesar enormous wealth and something even more dangerous: a veteran army loyal to him. Remember Marius? Soldiers looked to their general, not the Senate, for pay and for land. After eight years in Gaul, Caesar’s men knew exactly who their general was. That kind of loyalty doesn’t stay in Gaul.

cards.fact: Caesar wrote about himself in the third person.
cards.context: His Commentaries on the Gallic War describe Caesar’s deeds as if an observer were reporting them. It’s like writing your own glowing review in the voice of a neutral critic. Readers in Rome learned the war from Caesar’s point of view, and it read like plain history.

title: Crossing the Rubicon
objective: After this level you can explain why crossing the Rubicon meant civil war.
summary: In 49 BCE Caesar led his army across the Rubicon into Italy: civil war. He beat Pompey at Pharsalus in 48 BCE.

cards.headline: A small river. One step across. No way back.
cards.body: Crossing a river doesn’t usually start a war. In 49 BCE, this one did. The river was small. The rule it marked was not.

cards.headline: The boundary
cards.body: The Rubicon was a small river marking the boundary between Caesar’s province and Italy. The rule was simple: a general had to leave his army behind before crossing it. You could come home to Italy. Your army couldn’t. In January 49 BCE Caesar crossed with his army anyway. Sulla had marched his army on Rome in 88 BCE. Now Caesar was bringing his into Italy.

cards.headline: Caesar against Pompey
cards.body: The crossing started a civil war, with Pompey on the other side. Caesar defeated him at Pharsalus in Greece in 48 BCE. Pompey “the Great” fled to Egypt, where he was murdered. The river never got any bigger, but its name did. Today, “crossing the Rubicon” means passing a point of no return, like hitting send on a message you can’t unsend.

cards.fact: “Alea iacta est”: the die is cast.
cards.context: Caesar is said to have spoken these words as he crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE. Once a die is thrown, you can’t take the throw back. You can only wait and see how it lands.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 finale. Beware the Ides of March.
cards.body: From the Gracchi to Caesar: land fights, private armies, a march on Rome, a river crossed. It all built to a murder at a meeting of the Senate. Did the murder end the crisis?

cards.headline: Dictator for life
cards.body: In 44 BCE Julius Caesar was made dictator for life. Remember Level 12: a dictator was an emergency ruler for six months at most. “For life” is a very long emergency. Remember the oath from Level 9, too: Rome had sworn never again to let anyone be king. Dictator for life looked like the kingship Rome had sworn off, with a different name on the door.

cards.headline: The Ides of March
cards.body: On the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BCE, Caesar was stabbed to death at a meeting of the Senate. The plot was led by Brutus and Cassius, and Marcus Brutus claimed descent from the Brutus who had expelled Rome’s last king. History loves a rhyme. The conspirators hoped to restore the Republic. Instead, the murder led to more civil war. Killing one man couldn’t undo what Rome had learned since the Gracchi: armies loyal to generals, and violence in place of votes.

cards.headline: Caesar’s will named an heir almost no one expected: an 18-year-old.
cards.body: Caesar was dead, and his will handed a teenager his name. What can an 18-year-old do with a name? Quite a lot, it turned out.

cards.headline: The boy with the famous name
cards.body: Caesar’s will did more than leave his great-nephew a gift. It adopted Octavian, then 18, as his son and heir. Octavian took the name Gaius Julius Caesar, and he put it to work: it won over Caesar’s soldiers and supporters, who rallied to the man carrying it. Most heirs inherit the furniture. Octavian inherited Caesar’s fans, and a lot of them had swords.

cards.headline: Three men, again
cards.body: Remember the First Triumvirate, the informal deal between Caesar, Pompey and Crassus? In 43 BCE Octavian formed a second one with Mark Antony and Lepidus, and this time it was official: an alliance given legal power for five years. At Philippi in 42 BCE, Antony and Octavian defeated Caesar’s assassins, Brutus and Cassius, who both took their own lives. Two years after the Ides of March, the heir had outlasted the killers.

title: Antony and Cleopatra

summary: Antony ruled the East and allied with Cleopatra, last of the Ptolemies. When he gave her Roman lands, Octavian called him a traitor.

cards.headline: A Roman general and an Egyptian queen formed a partnership Rome called treason.
cards.body: Mark Antony ran Rome’s East. Cleopatra ruled Egypt. Together they handed Octavian exactly the story he needed.

cards.headline: The last of the Ptolemies
cards.body: Cleopatra VII was the last active ruler of Egypt’s Ptolemaic dynasty. Egyptian throne, Greek family: the Ptolemies were Greek-speaking, descended from one of Alexander the Great’s generals. And Roman generals were nothing new to her. She had been Julius Caesar’s ally and lover, and had a son, Caesarion, whom she said was Caesar’s. So when Antony came along, she had done this before.

cards.headline: Antony goes East
cards.body: After Philippi, Antony took charge of Rome’s eastern provinces and allied with Cleopatra. There was a small complication: in 40 BCE he had married Octavian’s sister, Octavia. He later left her for Cleopatra. Then, in 34 BCE, came the Donations of Alexandria, when Antony gave Roman lands in the East to Cleopatra and her children. Leaving your partner’s sister is awkward. Giving away Roman land is something else.

cards.fact: Octavian turned the romance into a weapon.
cards.context: He painted Antony as a traitor under the spell of a foreign queen, a Roman handing Roman land to her family. It worked: opinion in Rome turned against Antony. Octavian didn’t need to invent a scandal. Antony had supplied one.

title: Actium
objective: After this level you can explain the Battle of Actium and its consequences.
summary: In 31 BCE Agrippa’s fleet beat Antony and Cleopatra at Actium. Both died in 30 BCE, Egypt became Roman, and Octavian stood alone.

cards.headline: One sea battle decided who would rule the Roman world.
cards.body: Two sides, one sea battle off western Greece. Afterward, the Roman world had a single master.

cards.headline: War on a queen
cards.body: In 32 BCE Rome declared war, but not on Antony. It declared war on Cleopatra. The trick was in the label: Romans fighting Romans would be another civil war, while a war on a foreign queen looked like a foreign war. Same war, better label. For the fighting, Octavian relied on his closest friend, Marcus Agrippa, his leading general and admiral, who commanded his fleet at Actium.

cards.headline: Actium
cards.body: On 2 September 31 BCE, Octavian’s fleet defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium, off western Greece. The ending came the next year. In 30 BCE, as Octavian took Alexandria, Antony and Cleopatra both took their own lives. Remember Philippi, where Antony helped defeat Brutus and Cassius? Now he shared their ending.
cards.callout: Actium: 2 September 31 BCE

cards.headline: Master of the Roman world
cards.body: After Actium, Octavian was the sole master of the Roman world. In 43 BCE three men had shared power. Now there was one. He took Cleopatra’s kingdom too: Egypt became a Roman province under his personal control, and its grain helped feed Rome. The winner didn’t just get the throne room. He got the pantry.

title: Augustus, First Emperor
objective: After this level you can explain how Augustus ruled as emperor while claiming to restore the Republic.
summary: In 27 BCE Octavian “restored” the Republic and became Augustus. He kept the old offices but held the legions, and ruled for about 40 years.

cards.headline: He said he was giving power back. He kept almost all of it.
cards.body: It is one of history’s great magic tricks. Watch the hands: in 27 BCE, Octavian announced that the Republic was back.

cards.headline: The settlement of 27 BCE
cards.body: In 27 BCE Octavian claimed to restore the Republic, and the Senate gave him a new name: Augustus, “the revered one.” He called himself princeps, “first citizen,” and avoided the title of king. Remember Level 9? After the last king, rex was so hated that even Rome’s most powerful men steered clear of it. “First citizen” sounds like the person who arrives early to the town meeting. That was the point.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing here: the Republic’s forms stayed, but one man held the power.

cards.headline: Old forms, new power
cards.body: Here’s the trick. The Senate, consuls and elections all continued, so it still looked like the Republic. But Augustus controlled most of the legions and the key frontier provinces. Historians call his system the Principate, from princeps. The Republic’s furniture stayed in the house. He just owned the house. And he lived in it a long time: he ruled until his death in 14 CE, about 40 years as emperor.
cards.callout: Principate: rule by the princeps, the “first citizen”

cards.fact: Augustus wrote his own record of achievements.
cards.context: Called the Res Gestae, it was inscribed on bronze pillars outside his tomb, listing his victories, his buildings and his gifts to the Roman people. Most people leave a will. Augustus left a résumé.

title: The Pax Romana
objective: After this level you can describe the Pax Romana and what peace made possible.
summary: From Augustus to Marcus Aurelius, about 200 years of relative peace let trade, people and ideas move freely across the empire.

cards.headline: For about 200 years, most of the Roman world lived in peace.
cards.body: Not perfect peace, and not everywhere. But enough to change how people lived. So what did peace actually look like?

mascot.line: You don’t need both end dates. Remember: it starts with Augustus and lasts about 200 years.

cards.headline: The Roman peace
cards.body: The Pax Romana, “Roman peace,” was a stretch of about 200 years of relative peace and stability across the empire. It began with Augustus and is usually dated from 27 BCE to 180 CE, when the emperor Marcus Aurelius died. Notice the start date: 27 BCE, the year Octavian became Augustus. The first emperor didn’t just bring peace. Peace was his brand.
cards.callout: Pax Romana: 27 BCE to 180 CE

cards.headline: What peace made possible
cards.body: Peace is good for business. With the seas and roads safe, trade flowed across the Mediterranean, the sea Romans called Mare Nostrum, “our sea.” Goods, people and ideas moved from one end of the empire to the other, and cities grew and prospered. Safe roads are boring. Boring is wonderful for business.

cards.fact: The Pax Romana wasn’t free of war.
cards.context: Fighting went on at the frontiers. What the peace meant was that the empire’s interior was largely spared. If you lived in a city deep inside the empire, war was news from far away. If you were a soldier on the frontier, the Pax Romana was something that happened to other people.

title: A City of Marble
objective: After this level you can describe how Augustus rebuilt Rome and why buildings mattered politically.
summary: Augustus restored temples, Agrippa built baths and the first Pantheon, and the Ara Pacis celebrated peace. Every building sent a message.

cards.headline: “I found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble.”
cards.body: That’s Augustus bragging, as the historian Suetonius tells it. The surprising part: all that marble was also a message.

cards.headline: Building an image
cards.body: By his own count in the Res Gestae, Augustus restored 82 temples in a single year. That’s more than one a week. Why so many? His buildings advertised his piety and the peace he had brought, linking his rule to Rome’s gods. Remember the pax deorum from Level 7, Rome’s peace with the gods? Every restored temple was a billboard: this man keeps Rome right with heaven.

cards.headline: A friend who built
cards.body: Agrippa, the admiral whose fleet won at Actium, was also a builder. He paid for major public works in Rome, including baths and aqueducts, and he built the first Pantheon. Visit the domed Pantheon today and you’re standing in a later rebuilding under the emperor Hadrian, not Agrippa’s original. Win the war, then build the baths. Not a bad friend to have.

cards.fact: The Ara Pacis, the Altar of Augustan Peace, was dedicated in 9 BCE.
cards.context: Its carvings show members of Augustus’ family in procession: a family portrait in marble. The message is hard to miss. Here is the peace, and here is the family that brought it.

title: Virgil and the Aeneid
objective: After this level you can explain what the Aeneid is and why Augustus's Rome valued it.
summary: Virgil’s Aeneid follows the Trojan Aeneas to Italy. It gave Rome an epic to rival Homer’s, and Augustus’ family a heroic ancestor.

cards.headline: Rome’s greatest poem is about a refugee from a burning city.
cards.body: Not a conqueror, not a king. A man escaping the flames of Troy, guided by fate toward Italy. So why did Rome love this story so much?

cards.headline: The poem
cards.body: Virgil, who lived from 70 to 19 BCE, is widely regarded as the greatest poet of Augustan Rome. His Aeneid is an epic in 12 books, modeled on Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey. Its hero, the Trojan prince Aeneas, escapes burning Troy and, guided by fate, comes to Italy, where his descendants will found Rome. Rome’s great origin epic starts with a man who has lost his city.

cards.headline: A poem for Augustus
cards.body: Here’s why it suited the emperor so well. The Julian family, Caesar and Augustus included, claimed descent from Aeneas through his son Iulus. So Rome’s great epic doubled as Augustus’ family tree. And its hero is famous for pietas: dutiful devotion to the gods, his family and his country. Remember those 82 temples? Augustus was building the same image in marble.
cards.callout: Pietas: duty to gods, family and country

cards.fact: Virgil wanted the Aeneid burned.
cards.context: He died before finishing it and asked for the manuscript to be destroyed. Augustus had it published instead. Rome’s greatest poem survives because its author lost the argument.

title: Months Named for Emperors
objective: After this level you can explain the Julian calendar and how July and August got their names.
summary: Caesar’s Julian calendar of 46 BCE gave us 365 days and leap years. Two months were renamed for him and for Augustus.

cards.headline: Two of your months are named after Roman rulers.
cards.body: Every summer, your calendar turns to July, then August. That’s Julius Caesar, then Augustus. How did two Romans end up on your wall?

cards.headline: Caesar fixes the year
cards.body: In 46 BCE Julius Caesar introduced the Julian calendar, on the advice of the astronomer Sosigenes of Alexandria. It had 365 days, plus a leap day every fourth year. Why the extra day? A year is about 365 and a quarter days long, and three ordinary years plus one leap year average exactly 365.25. Caesar only got two years with his new calendar. The Ides of March came in 44 BCE.
cards.callout: Leap day: every fourth year

cards.headline: New names
cards.body: The Roman year once began in March, which solves a puzzle: Quintilis meant “fifth month,” and it was. It was renamed Julius, our July, in honor of Julius Caesar. Then, in 8 BCE, Sextilis was renamed Augustus, our August, in honor of Augustus. Adopted father and heir, side by side on every calendar you’ve ever owned.

cards.fact: The Julian calendar was slightly too long.
cards.context: By about 11 minutes a year. Tiny, but it added up, and the calendar drifted against the seasons. In 1582 Pope Gregory XIII replaced it with the Gregorian calendar we use today. Caesar’s calendar retired. His month didn’t.

title: Teutoburg Forest
objective: After this level you can explain the disaster in the Teutoburg Forest and how it fixed the Rhine frontier.
summary: In 9 CE Arminius led three legions under Varus into an ambush and destroyed them. Rome gave up on Germany and held the Rhine.

cards.headline: In 9 CE three Roman legions marched into a German forest. They never came out.
cards.body: And the man who led them to their doom was someone their general trusted.

cards.headline: The ambush
cards.body: In 9 CE, Germanic warriors led by Arminius destroyed three Roman legions under the governor Varus in the Teutoburg Forest. The shock was who Arminius was. He had served with the Roman army, and Varus trusted him. Arminius led him into an ambush. Remember Level 29: a legion had roughly 4,000 to 5,000 infantry. Three of them is some 12,000 to 15,000 soldiers, lost in one ambush.

cards.headline: The river becomes a border
cards.body: The disaster changed the map. Rome gave up its plans to conquer Germany east of the Rhine, and the river became a lasting frontier. How do we know where it happened? Archaeologists believe the battlefield lies near Kalkriese in Germany, where Roman weapons and coins have been found. One ambush in a forest, and a river became a border.

cards.fact: “Quintilius Varus, give me back my legions!”
cards.context: According to the historian Suetonius, Augustus cried out these words after hearing of the disaster. The sole master of the Roman world, and there was one thing he couldn’t get back.

title: Tiberius
objective: After this level you can describe the reign of Tiberius and the problem of succession.
summary: Tiberius, Augustus’ adopted stepson, ruled from 14 to 37 CE, much of it from Capri. Rome had no rule for choosing the next emperor.

cards.headline: Following Rome’s first emperor came with no instructions.
cards.body: Augustus built a brand-new job and never wrote down how to hand it on. So who gets it next, and who decides?

mascot.line: Hold on to this missing rule. Levels 60 and 82 both come back to it.

cards.headline: The heir who was left standing
cards.body: Augustus had no surviving son. He chose other successors first, and they died. So he adopted his stepson Tiberius as heir, and Tiberius became emperor on Augustus’ death in 14 CE, ruling until 37 CE. Here’s the catch: Rome never had a fixed law of succession. Each emperor had to choose his own heir, often by adoption. Imagine a family business where every owner rewrites the will from scratch.

cards.headline: Ruling from an island
cards.body: In his later years Tiberius withdrew to the island of Capri and ruled from there. Remote work, Roman style. But an absent boss leaves an empty office in Rome. Sejanus, commander of the Praetorian Guard, grew more and more powerful while Tiberius was away, until Tiberius had him executed in 31 CE. The man guarding the emperor had become the problem.

cards.fact: The Praetorian Guard was the emperor’s bodyguard, stationed in Rome itself.
cards.context: Soldiers that close could protect the emperor. As Sejanus showed, the man commanding them could also grow too strong. Keep an eye on this guard. It matters again in the very next level.

title: Caligula
objective: After this level you can separate what is known about Caligula from later rumor.
summary: Caligula, “little boot,” began popular in 37 CE and became autocratic. His own guard killed him in 41 CE. Many tales about him are hostile rumor.

cards.headline: Most of what you’ve heard about Caligula was written by people who hated him.
cards.body: So what can we actually trust? Start with a nickname, end with a murder, and read the gossip in between with care.

cards.headline: Little Boot
cards.body: Gaius became emperor in 37 CE, but everyone knows him by a nickname. As a child he lived in his father’s army camp, wearing a small soldier’s uniform, and the soldiers called him Caligula, “little boot.” Imagine ruling an empire under your childhood nickname. He was popular at first. Then his rule turned autocratic and extravagant.

mascot.line: Ask who wrote it before you ask if it’s true. You’ll use this again in Level 98.

cards.headline: Consider the source
cards.body: Here’s the trouble with Caligula’s legend: most accounts of him come from later writers who were hostile to him. So historians treat the wildest stories with caution. Take the famous one about his plan to make his horse a consul. It may be a joke, or an exaggeration. Before you ask whether a story is true, ask who wrote it.

title: Nero and the Great Fire

summary: Nero became emperor at 16. After the fire of 64 CE he blamed the Christians and built a palace on the ruins. His death in 68 CE ended Augustus’ line.

cards.headline: Rome burned for six days, and people have blamed Nero ever since.
cards.body: But what did he actually do? The real story has a teenage emperor, a scapegoat and a palace. It has no fiddle.

cards.headline: The teenage emperor
cards.body: Nero, Claudius’ adopted son, became emperor in 54 CE at the age of 16. Picture a 16-year-old handed the Roman world. It ended badly. Facing revolt, Nero took his own life in 68 CE, and with him ended the Julio-Claudian dynasty, the family line of Augustus. The family business had run out of family.

cards.headline: The Great Fire
cards.body: In 64 CE a great fire burned in Rome for six days. Of the city’s 14 districts, three were destroyed and seven more badly damaged. According to the historian Tacitus, Nero blamed the Christians in Rome and had many of them executed. Then, on land the fire had cleared, he built a vast palace, the Golden House. Not a great look for the man in charge.

cards.fact: Nero did not fiddle while Rome burned.
cards.context: That story is a later legend. The fiddle did not yet exist, and Tacitus says Nero was away at Antium when the fire began. It’s hard to play an instrument nobody has invented, in a city you’re not in.

title: The Year of the Four Emperors

What they had in common was an army: each claimant was backed by one. That was the year’s real lesson. The legions could make emperors, and they could unmake them.

cards.headline: The winner
cards.body: The last man standing was Vespasian, a general commanding in Judaea. He won the civil war and founded the Flavian dynasty. Looking back at Nero’s fall, the historian Tacitus named what it had exposed, a secret of empire: an emperor could be made somewhere other than Rome. The top job no longer had to be decided in the capital. It could march in from far away.

cards.fact: Vespasian came from a family of modest rank.

title: Pompeii and Vesuvius
objective: After this level you can explain the eruption of Vesuvius and why Pompeii is so valuable to historians.
summary: In 79 CE Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum. The ash that killed the towns preserved them, and Pliny the Younger described it all.

cards.headline: A volcano destroyed a town, and by burying it, saved it for us.
cards.body: The ash that ended life in Pompeii also sealed the town up, like a time capsule nobody meant to pack.

cards.headline: The eruption
cards.body: In 79 CE Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried two towns, Pompeii and Herculaneum. Titus was emperor, a year before he opened the Colosseum. Remarkably, we have a written account. Pliny the Younger described the eruption in letters to the historian Tacitus. His uncle, Pliny the Elder, died trying to rescue people.

cards.headline: A town frozen in time
cards.body: Pompeii was buried under several meters of ash and pumice. A disaster for its people, a gift for historians: the ash preserved buildings, paintings and everyday objects. Even the walls still talk. They carry painted notices and scratched graffiti, including election slogans. Imagine a town where the campaign posters never came down. Together it all gives historians a rare snapshot of ordinary Roman town life.

cards.fact: Plaster casts show victims in their final positions.
cards.context: The victims’ bodies left hollows in the ash. In the 1800s, excavators poured plaster into those hollows, and the casts recorded their final positions. The ash kept the town, and in a way it kept its people too.

title: Trajan's Empire at Its Largest
objective: After this level you can describe Trajan's conquests and the empire at its greatest extent.
summary: Trajan, born in Spain, conquered Dacia and pushed into Mesopotamia. In 117 CE the empire reached its greatest extent.

cards.headline: The empire reached its largest size under an emperor born in Spain.
cards.body: Rome’s biggest moment on the map came under the first emperor from outside Italy.

cards.headline: The best emperor
cards.body: Trajan, born in Spain, was the first emperor from outside Italy. He ruled from 98 to 117 CE, and the Senate gave him the title Optimus, “the best.” That’s not a nickname, it’s a job review. Every emperor so far had come from Italy. Now the empire’s own provinces could produce its ruler, and the Senate rated him top of the class.

cards.headline: Pushing the edges
cards.body: Trajan ruled during the Pax Romana, but that peace had edges. The empire’s interior was largely peaceful while fighting went on at the frontiers, and that’s where Trajan worked. He conquered Dacia, roughly modern Romania, in two wars ending in 106 CE. Then he pushed east as far as Mesopotamia. In 117 CE the empire reached its greatest extent. Rome would never be bigger on the map.

cards.fact: Trajan’s Column tells the story of the Dacian wars in stone.
cards.context: A spiral band of carvings winds up the column in Rome from base to top, showing the campaigns scene by scene. It’s a war report you read by walking in circles.

title: Hadrian and His Wall
objective: After this level you can explain why Hadrian consolidated the frontiers and built his wall.
summary: Hadrian gave up some conquests, toured the frontiers and fortified them. His wall ran about 118 km across northern Britain.

cards.headline: Hadrian’s answer to an empire too big to grow: guard its edges.
cards.body: Trajan left the empire at its biggest. His successor, Hadrian, went the other way: not how to grow it, but how to hold it.

cards.headline: Holding, not growing
cards.body: Hadrian, Trajan’s successor, ruled from 117 to 138 CE, and one of his big moves was handing land back: he gave up some of Trajan’s eastern conquests. Then he went to check on the rest. He spent much of his reign traveling through the provinces, inspecting armies and frontiers. An emperor doing site visits. In Rome he rebuilt the Pantheon, first built by Agrippa, as the domed building still standing today.

cards.headline: The wall
cards.body: Hadrian’s Wall, begun in 122 CE, ran about 118 km across northern Britain. It had small forts about every Roman mile, and larger forts along its length. That’s not a garden fence. It’s a frontier with a small fort every Roman mile, and it says out loud where the empire stops.

cards.fact: Hadrian was the first emperor regularly shown with a full beard.
cards.context: He loved Greek culture, and he wore it on his face: the beard was in the Greek style. Even his portraits tell you where his heart was.

title: Checkpoint: The Five Good Emperors
objective: After this level you can explain the era of the Five Good Emperors, ending with Marcus Aurelius.
summary: From 96 to 180 CE, emperors chosen by adoption gave Rome its steadiest era. Marcus Aurelius passed power to his son Commodus, and it ended.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale. Five emperors in a row who ruled well. Then it ended.
cards.body: Remember Rome’s missing rule for choosing the next emperor? For most of a century, Rome found a way around it. Then a father handed power to his son.

cards.headline: Choosing the best
cards.body: Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius, who ruled from 96 to 180 CE, are known as the Five Good Emperors. None of the first four left a surviving son, so each passed power to an adopted adult heir. (Even ancient writers doubted Trajan really adopted Hadrian before he died.) The historian Edward Gibbon called it the time when the human race was most happy and prosperous. Marcus Aurelius’ death in 180 CE is also where the Pax Romana is usually said to end.

cards.headline: The philosopher emperor
cards.body: The last of the five, Marcus Aurelius, was a Stoic philosopher. He wrote his private reflections, the Meditations, while on campaign: philosophy homework, done at the front. His reign had troubles too. A deadly epidemic, the Antonine Plague, swept the empire from about 165 CE. Then came the handover. Marcus was succeeded by his own son, Commodus, whose disastrous reign ended the era. After four chosen heirs, a son simply inherited.

title: A Day in the City
objective: After this level you can describe daily life in the city of Rome, from apartment blocks to the forum.
summary: Perhaps a million people crowded into Rome. Most rented rooms in risky apartment blocks; the rich lived in houses built around an atrium.

cards.headline: A million people, one city, and most of them had no bath at home.
cards.body: So where did all those Romans actually live? Mostly stacked on top of each other.

mascot.line: Hold on to these cramped apartments; the next few levels build on them.

cards.headline: Apartment life
cards.body: By the time of Augustus, Rome had perhaps around 1 million people, the largest city in the Western world. Most of them lived in insulae: crowded apartment blocks several stories high, usually without running water or private baths. The upper floors were the cheapest, and fire and collapse were constant dangers. Do the math: the cheaper your room, the more floors between you and the street when a fire broke out.
cards.callout: Insula: an apartment block

cards.headline: Houses and the Forum
cards.body: If you were rich, you skipped the stairs. Wealthy Romans lived in a domus, a private house built around an open hall called the atrium. Public life, for everyone, centered on the Forum, the once-marshy valley you met in Level 3. It packed temples, law courts, markets and platforms for speeches into one place. Picture a town square that was also the courthouse, the church and the mall.

cards.fact: Augustus gave Rome a force of night-time firefighters.
cards.context: He created the vigiles, freedmen who fought fires and patrolled the streets at night. He also capped new buildings at about 20 meters high. Rome’s apartment blocks finally had a ceiling.

title: Slavery in Rome
objective: After this level you can explain how slavery shaped Roman society and what freed slaves could become.
summary: Enslaved people, taken by war, piracy and birth, did every kind of work. Many were freed, and a citizen’s freed slave became a citizen.

cards.headline: In Rome, a doctor, a teacher and a miner could all be enslaved.
cards.body: Slavery reached into every corner of Roman life. So did something more surprising: a way out.

cards.headline: Property under the law
cards.body: Enslaved people made up a large share of the population of Roman Italy. War, piracy and trade fed the system, and a child born to an enslaved mother was enslaved too. Under Roman law an enslaved person was property, with no legal rights of their own. In the eyes of the law, a human being could be owned like a cart or a plow.

cards.headline: Every kind of work
cards.body: Enslaved people did every kind of work. Some dug in mines or labored on farms; others ran households. Some were teachers, doctors and secretaries, so the person teaching a rich family’s children could legally be property. But the story didn’t always end there. Romans often freed enslaved people, a practice called manumission.
cards.callout: Manumission: freeing an enslaved person

cards.fact: A citizen’s freed slave usually became a Roman citizen.
cards.context: Their children had full rights. Freedom could even lead to power: the emperor Claudius relied on freedmen, formerly enslaved people, as powerful officials. Owned in one generation, fully Roman in the next.

title: Bread and Circuses
objective: After this level you can explain the grain dole and public games and why rulers provided them.
summary: Rome fed about 200,000 citizens with free grain and staged huge free games. A poet mocked it as “bread and circuses.”

cards.headline: A Roman poet said his people wanted only two things: bread and circuses.
cards.body: He wasn’t paying them a compliment. So what were the bread and the circuses, and who was handing them out?

cards.headline: Free grain
cards.body: The bread was real. Rome gave free grain to many citizens living in the city, and under Augustus about 200,000 people received it. That’s a lot of mouths to feed. Much of that grain came from Egypt, a province under the emperor’s personal control. The emperor didn’t just run the city. He ran its pantry.

cards.headline: Free games
cards.body: The circuses were real too. Public games, ludi, began as religious festivals and grew into huge free entertainments. Worship had become a show. Who paid? Emperors and politicians, who funded games and food to win popularity and keep the city calm. Crowd control, served with a side of spectacle.

mascot.line: People often quote this as a catchy slogan. Juvenal meant it as a complaint.

cards.fact: “Bread and circuses” was a complaint.
cards.context: The poet Juvenal said the Roman people, who once handed out commands, now wanted only these two things. His jab: citizens who used to give the orders had settled for free food and shows.
