title: Gladiators
objective: After this level you can separate the reality of gladiator fights from popular myth.
summary: Gladiator fights began as funeral games. Most fighters were enslaved or condemned, fought in set types, and were often spared.

cards.headline: Thumbs down meant death? Probably not the way the movies show it.
cards.body: The real arena was stranger, and often less deadly, than the film version.

cards.headline: Who fought
cards.body: Gladiator fights probably began as funeral games to honor the dead, first recorded in Rome in 264 BCE. So Rome’s bloodiest show started as a way to mourn. Most gladiators were enslaved people, prisoners of war or condemned criminals. But some free men volunteered. Yes, a few people chose this job.

cards.headline: How they fought
cards.body: Gladiators fought in types with set equipment. The retiarius, armed with a net and trident, faced the helmeted secutor: a matchup, not a brawl. And gladiators were expensive to train, so many fights did not end in death. A beaten fighter could be spared. Nobody wants to lose an expensive investment in one afternoon.

cards.fact: No one knows exactly what the thumb meant.
cards.context: Roman writers mention a “turned thumb” deciding a gladiator’s fate, but its exact meaning is unknown. So when a movie emperor jabs his thumb down with total confidence, he knows more than historians do.

title: Chariot Racing
objective: After this level you can describe chariot racing, the Circus Maximus and the racing factions.
summary: The Circus Maximus held about 150,000 fans. Four color factions raced four-horse chariots seven laps, and rivalries could turn into riots.

cards.headline: Rome’s biggest crowds didn’t watch gladiators. They watched chariots.
cards.body: Rome had a venue that made the Colosseum look small. And its fans turned out to be more than spectators.

cards.headline: The Circus Maximus
cards.body: The Circus Maximus, Rome’s great racetrack, could hold about 150,000 spectators, about three times the Colosseum’s 50,000. A standard race was seven laps around the central barrier, the spina. The most prestigious races used quadrigae: chariots pulled by four horses. Seven laps, four horses, and a crowd the size of a city.

cards.headline: Reds, Whites, Blues and Greens
cards.body: Charioteers raced for four factions, the Reds, Whites, Blues and Greens, and each faction had passionate fans. Sound familiar? It’s the ancient version of wearing your team’s colors. A charioteer who won often enough could become rich and famous. The first sports celebrities drove at a gallop.

cards.fact: Racing fans nearly toppled an emperor.
cards.context: In 532 CE, fans of two factions, the Blues and the Greens, rioted together in Constantinople. The Nika revolt nearly toppled the emperor Justinian. When sports fans can shake a throne, they’re a political force. Not bad for a day at the races.

title: The Baths
objective: After this level you can explain what Roman baths were like and why they mattered socially.
summary: Cheap, heated public baths had hot, warm and cold rooms. Romans went to exercise, talk and do business, not just to wash.

cards.headline: For a Roman, the bath was the gym, the café and the office.
cards.body: Getting clean was almost the least of it.

mascot.line: You don’t need the Latin room names. Remember hot, warm, cold, heated from below.

cards.headline: Hot, warm, cold
cards.body: Large public baths, thermae, had rooms at three temperatures: the hot caldarium, the warm tepidarium and the cold frigidarium. The heat came from below. In the hypocaust, hot air from furnaces flowed under raised floors and up through the walls. Cold tiles on bare feet were not a Roman bather’s problem.
cards.callout: Hypocaust: underfloor heating

cards.headline: Why Romans went
cards.body: Remember Level 61: most Romans lived in apartment blocks without private baths. The public baths did far more than fill that gap. Romans exercised, talked, did business and relaxed there, and entry was cheap. The Baths of Caracalla, opened in the 3rd century CE, could serve about 1,600 bathers at a time. That’s a very crowded office.

cards.fact: Romans cleaned themselves without soap.
cards.context: Instead, bathers oiled their skin and scraped it clean with a curved metal tool, the strigil. Oil on, scrape off, and the dirt went with it. No bubbles, but it worked.

title: What Romans Ate
objective: After this level you can describe what rich and poor Romans ate, including garum.
summary: Most Romans ate grain, oil, wine and beans; the rich reclined at banquets. Almost everyone loved garum, a fermented fish sauce.

cards.headline: One of Rome’s most popular flavors came from fermented fish.
cards.body: Before you wince, see what else was on the table, and what definitely wasn’t.

cards.headline: Everyday food
cards.body: Most Romans lived on grain, eaten as porridge or bread, with olive oil, wine, vegetables and beans. Remember the apartment dwellers from Level 61? Many had no kitchen at home, so street counters called thermopolia sold them hot food. Ancient Rome had takeout.

cards.headline: Fish sauce and feasts
cards.body: Garum, a fermented fish sauce, was one of the most popular seasonings in the Roman world. Coastal factories, especially in Spain, made it, and clay jars called amphorae carried it around the empire. Fish sauce went everywhere Rome did. The rich dined differently: they held dinner parties in the triclinium, reclining on couches around a table. Dinner, lying down, with fish sauce.

cards.fact: No Roman ever ate a tomato.

title: Latin, the Language That Lived On

summary: Latin spread west with soldiers and settlers, and spoken Latin became Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian.

cards.headline: The Western Empire fell. Its language kept going.
cards.body: Latin didn’t vanish with Rome. It grew up into languages people still speak.

cards.headline: From Latium to the West
cards.body: Latin started small, in Latium, the region around Rome. It was the language of the Latins, the first Romans. As Rome grew, Latin spread through the western provinces with soldiers, settlers and officials. The East was different: Greek stayed the common language there. Rome ruled the East, but the East kept talking Greek.

cards.headline: Latin’s children
cards.body: Everyday spoken Latin, often called Vulgar Latin, didn’t stay put. It gradually developed into the Romance languages, including Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian. English isn’t one of them, but a large share of its vocabulary comes from Latin, much of it through French. So even this sentence is partly Roman.

cards.fact: Latin outlived the empire that spread it.

title: Roman Women

cards.body: Roman women lived with hard limits, and some found real power anyway.

cards.headline: Limits
cards.body: Start with the limits. Roman women could not vote or hold political office. Under early Roman law a woman needed a male guardian for legal matters, though the rule weakened over time. Girls from elite families were often married in their early to mid teens, usually to older men; most other girls probably married in their late teens. And remember the paterfamilias from Level 8? A daughter grew up under his legal power.

cards.headline: Wealth and influence
cards.body: Now the other side. Many Roman women owned property, ran businesses and inherited wealth. Influence didn’t need an office, either: Livia, the wife of Augustus, was one of the most influential people in Rome. Women also served as priestesses. The Vestal Virgins tended the sacred fire of Vesta, which was never allowed to go out. No vote, but Rome’s sacred fire was in their hands.

cards.fact: Julius Caesar’s daughter was simply called Julia.
cards.context: Roman daughters usually took a feminine form of the family name: Julius became Julia. Compare her father’s three-part name from Level 8, Gaius Julius Caesar. He got a small family tree; she got one word.

title: All Roads Lead to Rome
objective: After this level you can explain how Roman roads were built and why they mattered.
summary: Layered, drained and as straight as the land allowed, over 80,000 km of main roads carried armies first, then everyone else.

cards.headline: Rome laid more than 80,000 km of main roads. Who were they for?
cards.body: Not for sightseeing. The answer explains why Romans built them so carefully, one layer at a time.

cards.headline: Built like a layer cake
cards.body: A major Roman road wasn’t just paving stones laid on dirt. It was stacked in layers: a foundation of large stones, then gravel or rubble, then paving stones on top. It ran as straight as the ground allowed, and it was cambered, curved slightly, so rainwater drained off instead of sitting in puddles. Next time you notice the gentle hump in the middle of a street, you’re looking at a Roman idea.
cards.callout: Camber: a slight curve that sheds water

cards.headline: Built for marching
cards.body: Roman roads were built first for the army. A straight, solid, well-drained road let legions march quickly. Remember the Via Appia from Level 19, begun in 312 BCE to move armies south? That was the model. But once a road existed, everyone used it: traders, officials and the imperial post. Built for boots, used by everyone.

cards.fact: Roman roads came with distance markers: milestones.
cards.context: Milestones along the roads marked distances in Roman miles, each 1,000 paces long. So a traveler could count down the stones to the next town, the way you watch the signs tick down on a highway today.

title: Aqueducts
objective: After this level you can explain how aqueducts carried water to Roman cities using gravity.
summary: Aqueducts ran on a gentle downhill slope, mostly underground. By the 3rd century CE, 11 of them fed the city of Rome.

cards.headline: Rome brought water into the city without a single pump.
cards.body: No engines, no waterwheels. Just one force that never takes a day off.

mascot.line: People picture the arches. But most of an aqueduct ran underground or at ground level.

cards.headline: Downhill all the way
cards.body: An aqueduct was a very long, very gentle slide. Water flowed by gravity along a steady downhill slope from springs in the hills. And the famous arches? They’re the exception. Most of an aqueduct’s length ran underground or at ground level. Arches only carried it across valleys, where the ground dropped away but the slope had to stay steady. Keep the slope steady, and the water keeps coming.

cards.headline: Water for a city
cards.body: Rome’s first aqueduct, the Aqua Appia, was built in 312 BCE by Appius Claudius, the same man who began the Appian Way. Roads and water in the same year: busy man. More followed, and by the 3rd century CE, 11 aqueducts supplied the city. Water mattered so much that Rome had a water commissioner. Around 97 CE that was Frontinus, who wrote a whole book about the aqueducts.

cards.fact: The Pont du Gard still stands in southern France.
cards.context: It’s one of those valley-crossing bridges: three tiers of arches, about 49 m high, all to keep the water on its gentle downhill slope.

title: Roman Concrete
objective: After this level you can explain what made Roman concrete so durable.
summary: Lime and volcanic ash made a concrete that set underwater and shaped domes. Lumps of lime even helped it heal its own cracks.

cards.headline: Romans built harbors out in the sea, with concrete that set underwater.
cards.body: How do you make something harden while it’s soaking wet? The secret came out of a volcano.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing: volcanic ash let Roman concrete set even underwater.

cards.headline: Ash and lime
cards.body: Roman concrete mixed lime with volcanic ash, called pozzolana, plus chunks of rock or brick. The ash is named after Pozzuoli, near Naples, where it was dug. It was the key ingredient: concrete made with it could set even underwater. So Romans could do something that sounds like a terrible idea, putting fresh concrete into the sea, and build harbors there.
cards.callout: Pozzolana: volcanic ash from near Naples

cards.headline: New shapes, hidden core
cards.body: Concrete didn’t just survive the sea. It let Romans build arches, vaults and domes on a scale never seen before. You’d rarely notice it, though. Walls were usually faced with brick or stone, so the concrete core was hidden from view. Rome showed you the neat outfit and kept the muscle underneath.

cards.fact: Roman concrete could repair itself.
cards.context: A 2023 study found that lumps of lime in the mix could react with water to seal cracks, helping the concrete last. Water, the enemy of most buildings, was helping these ones heal.

title: The Pantheon
objective: After this level you can describe the Pantheon and its record-breaking dome.
summary: Hadrian’s Pantheon has the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, lit only by its oculus. As a church it survived intact.

cards.headline: The largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world was built by the Romans.
cards.body: Remember the volcanic concrete from Level 73? This is what it could do at full stretch.

cards.headline: A ball inside a building
cards.body: Pantheon means “of all the gods.” The building standing today is Hadrian’s rebuilding of Agrippa’s first Pantheon. Its dome, about 43 m across, is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. And the proportions are perfect: the height from the floor to the top of the dome equals its diameter. So a complete sphere 43 m wide would fit inside, resting on the floor.

cards.headline: Light and lightness
cards.body: Look up and there’s a hole in the roof. The oculus, about 8 m wide, is the building’s only source of natural light. The dome itself slims down as it rises: it gets thinner toward the top, and lighter stone was mixed into the concrete higher up. Less weight up high means less weight pressing down on everything below.
cards.callout: Oculus: the open “eye” at the top

cards.fact: The Pantheon survived by changing religion.
cards.context: In 609 CE the temple “of all the gods” became a Christian church, which helped it survive intact. New job, same building.

title: Running the Provinces
objective: After this level you can explain how governors, taxes and local elites ran the provinces.
summary: Governors ran provinces, split by Augustus between the Senate and himself. Taxes came from a census, and local elites did most of the work.

cards.headline: Rome ran a vast empire with surprisingly few officials.
cards.body: So who did all the work? Mostly, other people.

cards.headline: Who got which province
cards.body: Augustus split the provinces in two. Peaceful ones got governors chosen by the Senate. Frontier provinces, the ones with armies, were run by his own deputies. Notice which half he kept: the half with the soldiers. Either way, every province paid taxes on land and on people, and a census counted them for taxation. Being counted by Rome meant being charged by Rome.

cards.headline: Local help
cards.body: Here’s the few-officials secret. Rome relied on local elites to govern their own cities and collect taxes. Under the Republic, tax collection had often been contracted out to private companies of publicani instead, and they were notorious for abuses. Handing a for-profit company the job of squeezing your subjects: what could go wrong?
cards.callout: Publicani: private tax contractors

cards.fact: Pontius Pilate was a provincial governor.
cards.context: He was the Roman prefect who governed Judaea from 26 to 36 CE. A name most people know, in a job most people never think about.

title: Becoming Roman
objective: After this level you can explain Roman citizenship and how it spread to all free people in 212.
summary: Citizenship brought legal privileges. It spread to Italy, then to towns, soldiers and individuals, until Caracalla gave it to almost all free people in 212 CE.

cards.headline: In 212 CE, one emperor made almost every free person a Roman citizen.
cards.body: For centuries, citizenship had been something you were granted or earned. What made it worth having?

cards.headline: What citizenship meant
cards.body: Roman citizens had legal privileges, such as the right to appeal to Rome and protection from certain punishments. Think of it as a passport that doubled as a shield. According to the Book of Acts, Paul of Tarsus, a Roman citizen, used exactly that shield: his right to appeal to the emperor.

cards.headline: How it spread
cards.body: Italy got it the hard way. During the Social War of 91–88 BCE, Rome granted citizenship to its Italian allies, which helped end the revolt. After that it spread through the provinces by grants to towns, to individuals and to soldiers. Non-citizen soldiers, the auxiliaries, received it after about 25 years of service. And as Level 62 showed, a person freed by a Roman citizen usually became a citizen too.

cards.fact: In 212 CE Caracalla made almost every free person a citizen.
cards.context: After centuries of grants, one town, one veteran at a time, being Roman became a status shared across the whole empire. The members’ club had opened its doors to nearly everyone.

title: Roman Law
objective: After this level you can explain the key ideas of Roman law and how they reached modern legal systems.
summary: Jurists developed Roman law for a thousand years after the Twelve Tables. Justinian’s code carried it into the law of much of the world.

cards.headline: If you live in France or Brazil, your law has Roman roots.
cards.body: The trail runs through Roman lawyers’ opinions and one emperor’s giant collection.

cards.headline: Lawyers who shaped the law
cards.body: Rome first wrote its laws down around 450 BCE, in the Twelve Tables. Then its legal experts, the jurists, wrote opinions that developed and explained the law. Some of their ideas now feel like common sense. Take the burden of proof: it rests on the person who makes a claim, not on the one who denies it. If your neighbor says you owe him money, he has to prove it. You don’t have to prove you don’t.
cards.callout: Burden of proof: whoever claims must prove

cards.headline: Justinian’s code
cards.body: In the 6th century CE the emperor Justinian had Roman law collected into the Corpus Juris Civilis, the “body of civil law.” That code shaped the civil law systems used across continental Europe, Latin America and many other countries. So a court in Paris or São Paulo still runs on ideas an emperor had collected about 1,500 years ago.

cards.fact: Legal English is full of Latin.
cards.context: Many legal terms are Latin words, such as alibi, which means “elsewhere.” So “I have an alibi” really just says “I was elsewhere.”

title: Money and Trade
objective: After this level you can describe Roman coins, trade routes and the economy of the Mediterranean.
summary: The silver denarius carried the emperor’s face everywhere. Amphorae carried wine, oil and fish sauce, and traders reached India.

cards.headline: In Rome there is a hill made entirely of broken jars.
cards.body: To see how it got there, follow the money, and the olive oil.

mascot.line: Hold on to that shrinking silver. It comes back in the crisis of Level 81.

cards.headline: Coins with a message
cards.body: The denarius, a silver coin, was the standard Roman coin for centuries. It was also a tiny billboard: coins carried the emperor’s portrait and short messages, spreading his image across the empire. Every time you paid, you saw the boss. Then came the catch. Over time emperors reduced the silver in the denarius, and by the 3rd century CE it held very little. Same coin, same face, less and less silver.

cards.headline: Goods on the move
cards.body: Wine, olive oil and fish sauce moved around the Mediterranean in amphorae, clay jars made for shipping. Think of them as Rome’s cardboard boxes. And trade didn’t stop at the sea’s edge: Roman traders sailed to India, and Chinese silk reached Rome through many middlemen along the Silk Road.
cards.callout: Amphora: a two-handled shipping jar

cards.fact: Monte Testaccio is an artificial hill.
cards.context: It’s made of fragments of millions of broken olive oil amphorae, piled up in Rome itself. Picture how much olive oil that was, and then remember it’s only the empties.

title: Life on the Frontier
objective: After this level you can describe forts, soldiers and communities on the Roman frontier.
summary: Auxiliaries held standard forts along the limes. Towns grew beside them, and the Vindolanda tablets let us read their letters.

cards.headline: At a fort in northern Britain, a commander’s wife sent a birthday invitation.
cards.body: Life on the edge of the empire wasn’t all marching and watching. So who actually lived out there?

cards.headline: Forts on the limes
cards.body: The fortified frontier of the empire was called the limes. Much of it was held by auxiliaries, non-citizen soldiers recruited from the provinces: the same soldiers who received Roman citizenship after about 25 years (Level 76). Their forts followed a standard plan: a rectangle with rounded corners, four gates and a headquarters building at the center. Seen one Roman fort? You could find your way around the next.
cards.callout: Limes: the fortified frontier

cards.headline: Towns beside the forts
cards.body: Where there were soldiers, other people followed. Civilian settlements grew up beside frontier forts, with traders, craftsmen and soldiers’ families. On Hadrian’s Wall, small forts stood about every Roman mile, with larger forts along its length. A frontier, it turns out, was also a neighborhood.

cards.fact: We can read letters written on the frontier.
cards.context: At Vindolanda, a fort near Hadrian’s Wall, archaeologists found more than a thousand wooden writing tablets. Among them is the invitation from the start of this level, from one commander’s wife to another. It’s everyday frontier life, in the frontier’s own words.

title: Checkpoint: How Rome Held an Empire
objective: After this level you can explain how roads, law, citizenship, the army and trade held the empire together.
summary: Roads, a shared army, citizenship, law and trade held the empire together, and Roman ways spread through the provinces.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 finale. How do you hold together an empire from Britain to Egypt?
cards.body: Not with soldiers alone. You’ve already met most of the answer in this chapter.

cards.headline: More than force
cards.body: Rome held its empire together with roads, a shared army, citizenship, law and trade, not by force alone. It also ran its provinces with few officials: local elites ran their own cities and collected the taxes. And in 212 CE almost every free person became a citizen. The strongest glue wasn’t fear. It was citizenship and shared law: being Roman.

cards.headline: Becoming Roman
cards.body: Historians call the spread of Roman language, culture and ways of life in the provinces Romanization. You could see it: towns across the West built forums, baths and amphitheaters on the Roman model. You could hear it too, as Latin spread through the western provinces with soldiers, settlers and officials. In the East, Greek stayed the common language.

title: The Crisis of the Third Century
objective: After this level you can explain the chaos of the third century, when emperors rose and fell rapidly.
summary: From 235 to 284 CE, more than 20 emperors came and went, an emperor was captured, and the empire split in three before Aurelian reunited it.

cards.headline: More than 20 emperors in about 50 years. Most of them were murdered.
cards.body: Remember 69 CE, when the legions learned they could make and unmake emperors? For half a century, they did it again and again. Becoming emperor was a promotion with a very short life expectancy.

cards.headline: Everything at once
cards.body: From 235 to 284 CE, the Crisis of the Third Century, the empire suffered civil wars, invasions, plague and economic trouble, all at the same time. Even the money went bad. Emperors had kept reducing the silver in the denarius until the coin held very little, and prices soared. Imagine every new batch of coins holding a little less of the metal that made them worth anything. That was Roman money in the third century.

cards.headline: An emperor taken prisoner
cards.body: Then came the low point. In 260 CE the emperor Valerian was captured by the Persian king Shapur I. No Roman emperor had ever been taken prisoner by a foreign enemy before. The empire itself came apart, too. For a time it split into three: a breakaway Gallic Empire in the west, Rome in the middle, and Palmyra under Queen Zenobia in the east. One empire, three maps.

cards.fact: Aurelian put the pieces back together.
cards.context: In the 270s the emperor Aurelian reunited the three pieces into one empire. He also built new walls around Rome itself. A reunited empire whose capital needed fresh walls: that is the third century in a single picture.

title: Diocletian Divides the Empire
objective: After this level you can explain Diocletian's reforms and the Tetrarchy.
summary: Diocletian ended the crisis in 284 CE with four emperors, smaller provinces and price controls, then retired to his palace at Split.

cards.headline: One emperor wasn’t enough. Diocletian tried four.
cards.body: After half a century of murdered emperors, Diocletian’s fix was bold. If one ruler can’t guard everything, hire more rulers.

cards.headline: Rule of four
cards.body: Diocletian became emperor in 284 CE and ended the half century of crisis. His big idea was the Tetrarchy, “rule of four”: two senior emperors, called Augusti, and two junior ones, called Caesars. With four emperors, one could be near every threatened frontier. The junior Caesars also gave the empire a planned succession. That fixed an old problem: Rome never had a fixed law of succession, so every emperor had to pick his own heir. Now the next emperors were lined up in advance.
cards.callout: Tetrarchy: two Augusti and two Caesars

cards.headline: Smaller pieces, fixed prices
cards.body: Diocletian also split the provinces into smaller units and separated civil from military command, so the man running a province was no longer the man leading its troops. Then he took on inflation. In 301 CE his Edict on Maximum Prices tried to stop it by fixing prices by law. It failed. It turns out you can’t order a price to stay put.

cards.fact: Diocletian did what no emperor had done: he retired.
cards.context: In 305 CE he stepped down voluntarily, the first Roman emperor to do so, and moved to his palace at Split, in modern Croatia. After an age when most emperors left office by being killed, this one simply packed up and left.

In an empire of many gods, that got noticed.

cards.fact: Early churches looked after their own.
cards.context: Each Christian community was led by a bishop, and it cared for its own poor, widows and sick. A church wasn’t only a place to pray. It was a support network with someone in charge.

title: Persecution
objective: After this level you can explain why and when Christians were persecuted by the Roman state.
summary: Persecution was local and sporadic until Decius in 250 CE. Diocletian’s Great Persecution from 303 CE was the harshest.

cards.headline: Why would a tolerant empire of many gods persecute one group?
cards.body: The answer isn’t really about what Christians believed. It’s about what they refused to do.

mascot.line: Keep this: the trouble was what Christians refused to do. It’s Level 7’s pax deorum again.

cards.headline: Why Christians were targeted
cards.body: Roman religion was about doing the rituals right to keep the pax deorum, the peace with the gods. So when Christians refused to sacrifice to the gods and the emperor, it looked like disloyalty, and Romans feared it would break the peace with the gods. Picture a neighbor refusing to help mend the dam everyone lives behind. Still, for most of the first two centuries persecution was local and sporadic, not constant. Even Nero, as Tacitus tells it, blamed the Christians of Rome for the fire of 64 CE, not Christians everywhere.

cards.headline: Empire-wide
cards.body: Then the crisis century changed the rules. In 250 CE the emperor Decius ordered everyone in the empire to sacrifice to the gods: the first empire-wide persecution. Refusing was no longer a local matter. The worst came last. The Great Persecution under Diocletian, from 303 CE, was the harshest the Christians faced. Yes, the same Diocletian who reorganized the whole empire.

cards.fact: Trajan told a governor not to hunt Christians.
cards.context: Pliny the Younger, governing a province, asked Trajan how to treat Christians. Trajan’s answer: don’t hunt them out, but if they are accused and refuse to recant, punish them. Don’t go looking, but don’t look away. Those who died were honored as martyrs, from a Greek word meaning “witness.”

cards.headline: A new capital

title: Julian the Apostate
objective: After this level you can describe Julian's attempt to restore the old religion.
summary: Constantine’s nephew Julian tried to bring back the old gods in 361 CE. He died in Persia in 363, and his program died with him.

cards.headline: One emperor tried to turn the clock back to the old gods.
cards.body: Half a century after the Milvian Bridge, Constantine’s own nephew set out to undo his uncle’s work.

cards.headline: The last pagan emperor
cards.body: Julian, Constantine’s nephew, became sole emperor in 361 CE. His uncle had backed Christianity; Julian rejected it, and tried to restore worship of the traditional gods. He was the last Roman emperor to follow the old gods. The old religion got one more emperor on its side, and then no more.

cards.headline: A short reign
cards.body: Christians gave him the name he’s still known by: Julian the Apostate. An apostate is someone who abandons their faith. His revival never got time to take root. He was killed on campaign against Persia in 363 CE, about two years after becoming sole emperor, and his religious program died with him.
cards.callout: Apostate: someone who abandons their faith

cards.fact: Julian banned Christians from teaching classical literature.
cards.context: Picture a school where the old poets and philosophers are on the syllabus, but Christian teachers aren’t allowed to teach them. That was Julian’s rule for classical literature.

title: A Christian Empire
objective: After this level you can explain how Christianity became the empire's official religion under Theodosius.
summary: In 380 CE Theodosius made Nicene Christianity the official religion; in the 390s temples closed. After his death in 395 the empire split.

cards.headline: Within a lifetime of the Great Persecution, Christianity became the law.
cards.body: From hunted faith to official religion. Here’s how the tables turned.

cards.headline: The official religion
cards.body: In 380 CE, under Theodosius I, Nicene Christianity became the official religion of the empire. Then the old religion was shut down. In the 390s Theodosius banned sacrifices and closed temples. Even the sacred fire of Vesta, which the Vestal Virgins had tended and never allowed to go out, was put out, and the Vestals were disbanded. The fire that must never go out: out.

cards.headline: Church and emperor
cards.body: The church could now challenge an emperor. After a massacre at Thessalonica, Bishop Ambrose of Milan made Theodosius do public penance. The ruler of the Roman world, saying sorry in public, on a bishop’s orders. Theodosius was also the last emperor to rule both halves of the empire. After his death in 395 CE, it was divided between his two sons.

cards.fact: The ancient Olympics ended in a Christian empire.
cards.context: They are traditionally said to have ended in 393 CE under Theodosius, in the same decade the temples were closed.

title: Disaster at Adrianople
objective: After this level you can explain the Gothic victory at Adrianople and why it mattered.
summary: Goths fleeing the Huns crossed the Danube in 376 CE, rebelled against mistreatment and destroyed a Roman army at Adrianople in 378.

cards.headline: In 378 CE a Roman emperor died on the battlefield against the Goths.
cards.body: It started with refugees at a river.

cards.headline: Refugees become rebels
cards.body: The trouble began far from Rome. The Huns, nomadic horsemen from the Eurasian steppes, were pushing west and driving other peoples before them. In 376 CE Goths fleeing the Huns were allowed to cross the Danube into the empire. Then Roman officials mistreated and exploited them, and the Goths rebelled. Rome had let them in, then given them a reason to fight.

cards.headline: The battle
cards.body: Two years later came Adrianople. In 378 CE the Goths destroyed a Roman army there, and the emperor Valens was killed. Gothic cavalry arriving during the battle played a decisive part in the defeat. Rome had lost armies before: in 9 CE, three legions under Varus were wiped out in the Teutoburg Forest. This time the emperor himself died.

cards.fact: Afterwards, the Goths stayed.
cards.context: Gothic groups settled inside the empire as allies under their own leaders. Rebels one year, allies the next, with their own commanders inside Rome’s borders. It was a new arrangement, and a risky one.

title: Checkpoint: A Changed Empire
objective: After this level you can explain how the empire of 395 differed from the empire of Augustus.
summary: By 395 CE the empire was Christian, ruled by distant monarchs, split in two and defended partly by Goths under their own leaders.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 finale. Would Augustus have recognized the empire of 395?
cards.body: Line up the empire of 395 CE against the one Augustus left. Four big changes made it a different world.

cards.headline: A different empire
cards.body: By 395 CE the empire was Christian. It was divided into East and West, with two capitals: Rome, and Constantinople, dedicated in 330 CE. After Theodosius died in 395 CE, his two sons divided it between them. And it was defended partly by Germanic allies under their own leaders, like the Goths who settled inside the empire after Adrianople. Three changes down.

cards.headline: Lord, not first citizen
cards.body: The fourth change was the emperor himself. Augustus had called himself princeps, “first citizen,” and avoided the title of king. Later emperors dropped the modesty and ruled openly as absolute monarchs, surrounded by elaborate court ceremony. Historians sometimes call this the Dominate, from dominus, “lord.” From first citizen to lord: Augustus might not recognize the job.

title: The Sack of Rome, 410
objective: After this level you can explain Alaric's sack of Rome and its shock to the Roman world.
summary: In 410 CE Alaric’s Visigoths plundered Rome for three days, the first foreign capture in about 800 years. Augustine answered with The City of God.

cards.headline: In 410 CE, Rome fell to an enemy for the first time in about 800 years.
cards.body: The last time, it was Brennus and his Gauls, back in about 390 BCE. So how did the city that took the whole world end up taken?

mascot.line: This is Level 89’s risky arrangement coming due.

cards.headline: Alaric at the gates
cards.body: The Visigoths weren’t strangers at the door. Since the years after Adrianople, Gothic groups had lived inside the empire as allies under their own leaders, a risky arrangement. For a while, the western empire’s leading general, Stilicho, held the Visigoth leader Alaric off. Then, in 408 CE, Stilicho was executed. In 410 CE Alaric’s Visigoths sacked Rome and plundered it for three days. The guard went first. Two years later, so did the city.

cards.headline: A shock to the world
cards.body: The scholar Jerome put it in one line: the city which had taken the whole world was itself taken. Then came the blame. Christianity had been the empire’s official religion since 380 CE, and some pagans said the sack was the price of abandoning the old gods. Augustine of Hippo wrote The City of God partly to answer them. One raid on one city, and the argument went all the way up to heaven.

cards.fact: The emperor wasn’t even home.
cards.context: By 410 CE the western emperor Honorius lived at Ravenna, a city protected by marshes, not in Rome. So while Alaric’s men plundered the old capital, the emperor sat safely behind a swamp. Not a glamorous address, but a hard one to storm.

title: Attila and the Huns
objective: After this level you can describe the Huns under Attila and their impact on the empire.
summary: Attila squeezed gold from the East, was stopped in Gaul in 451 CE and turned back from Italy in 452. His empire died with him in 453.

cards.headline: Christian writers called him the “Scourge of God.”
cards.body: Attila, king of the Huns, earned that name the hard way. Here’s how, and why his power didn’t outlive him.

cards.headline: King of the Huns
cards.body: Remember the Huns from Level 89, the steppe horsemen whose push west drove the Goths across the Danube? Attila ruled them from 434 to 453 CE, at first sharing power with his brother Bleda. He raided the Eastern Empire and forced it to pay him large amounts of gold. For once, the Romans were the ones handing over the treasure.

cards.headline: Stopped twice
cards.body: In 451 CE Attila invaded Gaul. A Roman and Visigothic army under the general Aetius stopped him at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains. Yes, Visigoths: 41 years after sacking Rome, they fought on Rome’s side. In 452 CE Attila invaded Italy instead. Pope Leo I met him, and Attila withdrew. A general stopped him in Gaul; a pope met him in Italy.

cards.fact: Attila’s empire died with him.
cards.context: Attila died in 453 CE, and his empire of many peoples soon fell apart. It had depended on Attila himself to hold it together. Without him, the Scourge of God’s empire lasted about as long as a sandcastle at high tide.

title: 476: The Last Western Emperor
objective: After this level you can explain what happened in 476 and why historians debate its importance.
summary: After the Vandal sack of 455 CE, Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476 and ruled Italy as king. Historians debate how much changed.

cards.headline: The last western emperor bore the names of Rome’s founder and first emperor.
cards.body: Romulus, the founder, and Augustus, the name the Senate gave Octavian, Rome’s first emperor. And “Augustulus” means “little Augustus.” The empire ended on a diminutive.

cards.headline: The Vandals
cards.body: Before the last emperor, one more sack. In 455 CE the Vandals sacked Rome for two weeks. Alaric’s Goths had managed three days. The Vandals also left behind something that outlasted the damage: their name. It gave us the word vandalism. Every scribbled-on bus shelter carries a little fifth-century history.

cards.headline: 476 CE
cards.body: In 476 CE the Germanic commander Odoacer deposed the young western emperor Romulus Augustulus. Then he did something odd. He did not make himself emperor. He sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople and ruled Italy as king. That’s the usual date given for the fall of the Western Empire. The crown jewels went east, and Italy got a king.

mascot.line: Keep this: 476 is a handy marker, not the day the lights went out.

cards.fact: Did Rome really fall in 476?
cards.context: Many historians see 476 CE as a convenient marker rather than a sudden end, since life in Italy went on much as before for many people. An empire ended, and for many people the next day looked a lot like the one before.

title: Why Did Rome Fall?
objective: After this level you can compare the main explanations for the fall of the Western Empire.
summary: Invasions, civil wars and the loss of Africa broke the West. Gibbon blamed Christianity and lost virtue; others see a transformation.

cards.headline: Historians have given many answers to why the West fell. Here are the big ones.
cards.body: The West fell in 476 CE. Fine. But why? Historians have proposed many answers, and one twist: maybe “fall” is the wrong word.

cards.headline: Outside and inside
cards.body: Start with the squeeze. From outside, pressure from Germanic peoples and the Huns stretched the western army beyond its limits. From inside, repeated civil wars between Roman generals weakened the West further. Then came the money. When the Vandals captured Carthage in 439 CE, the West lost its richest tax base and a major grain supply. Enemies at the door, fights in the house, and an empty pantry.

cards.headline: Fall or transformation?
cards.body: The classic answer came from Edward Gibbon, the historian who called the age of the Five Good Emperors the happiest (Level 60). His The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire blamed, in part, the rise of Christianity and a loss of civic virtue. Some historians today tell it differently: not a sudden collapse, but a transformation into the kingdoms of medieval Europe. Less a house falling down, more a house slowly remodeled by new owners.

cards.fact: The richer half survived.
cards.context: The East was richer and more populous than the West, which helps explain why it outlived the West by nearly a thousand years (you’ll meet it next level). Two halves of one empire, and the one with more money and more people was the one still standing.

cards.headline: The fall: debated
learned: Invasions stretched the western army
Civil wars weakened the West

title: The Empire That Didn't Fall
objective: After this level you can explain how the Eastern Roman Empire lasted until 1453.
summary: The Greek-speaking East called itself Roman. Justinian won back Italy and built Hagia Sophia; Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453.

cards.headline: The Roman Empire lasted until 1453, if you count the East.
cards.body: The eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, outlived the West by nearly a thousand years. So when did Rome really end? Depends which half you ask.

mascot.line: “Byzantine” is our label. Its people simply called themselves Romans.

cards.headline: Romans in the East
cards.body: Historians call the Eastern Roman Empire the Byzantine Empire. That’s our label, not theirs: its people called themselves Romans. Their capital was Constantinople, which Constantine dedicated in 330 CE. Over time, though, Greek replaced Latin as the language of its government. So picture it: Romans, running the Roman Empire, in Greek.

cards.headline: Justinian’s ambition
cards.body: In the 6th century CE, the emperor Justinian reconquered Italy and North Africa, for a time. The old West was briefly Roman again. He also had Roman law collected into the Corpus Juris Civilis, the “body of civil law.” And he built the great church of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, finished in 537 CE. Land, law and a landmark: not a bad record for a “fallen” empire.

cards.fact: Constantinople fell in 1453 CE.
cards.context: Sultan Mehmed II led the Ottoman capture of the city, more than a thousand years after Constantine dedicated it in 330 CE. That’s the last page of Roman history, if you count the East. The city itself carried on under a new name: today it’s Istanbul.

title: Integration: Rome in Our Laws and Governments
objective: After this level you can connect Roman institutions to modern republics and legal systems.
summary: Senates, capitols, vetoes and balanced constitutions come from Rome, and Justinian’s code underlies civil law across much of the world.

cards.headline: Every time a president vetoes a bill, they are speaking Latin.
cards.body: Veto is Latin for “I forbid.” And that’s just one of the things Rome left inside modern governments. Let’s count them.

cards.headline: Names we kept
cards.body: Start with the names. Rome’s Senate began as a council of elders advising the king, and the United States Senate takes its name from it. The US Capitol is named after Rome’s Capitoline Hill, home of its greatest temple, dedicated to Jupiter, king of the gods. And veto? A Roman tribune could block other magistrates by declaring “Veto.” Today the word still means the power to block laws, as when a US president vetoes a bill. Same word, same job.

cards.headline: Ideas we kept
cards.body: Names are easy to borrow. Ideas matter more. The Greek historian Polybius praised Rome’s government as a mix: consuls like monarchs, a Senate of aristocrats, and assemblies for the people, each checking the others. The framers of the US Constitution studied the Roman Republic and its balance between different parts of government. And Justinian’s code shaped the civil law systems of continental Europe, Latin America and many other countries. Rome’s rules still run courtrooms Rome never saw.

title: Integration: Rome in Our Words, Calendars and Cities
objective: After this level you can trace Rome's legacy in languages, calendars, architecture and city planning.
summary: Roman towns became London and Paris, Roman columns became capitols and banks, and July and August still honor Caesar and Augustus.

cards.headline: You can see Rome in a city map, a bank front and a calendar.
cards.body: The empire is long gone. Its fingerprints aren’t. Let’s go looking for them.

cards.headline: Cities and buildings
cards.body: Many European cities grew from Roman towns or forts, including London, Paris, Cologne and Vienna. Many Roman towns were laid out on a grid, with two main streets crossing at right angles. Much later, neoclassical architecture copied Roman columns, domes and temple fronts in buildings across Europe and the Americas. Next time you pass a bank with columns out front, you’re looking at a Roman idea wearing a suit.

cards.headline: Words and time
cards.body: Everyday spoken Latin kept changing until it became Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian. English isn’t one of those Romance languages, but a large share of its vocabulary comes from Latin, much of it through French. Now check a calendar. July is named for Julius Caesar, and August for Augustus. Rome’s two most famous names, still sitting side by side every year.

cards.fact: “E pluribus unum”: out of many, one.
cards.context: Latin mottoes still appear on seals and coins. This one sits on the Great Seal of the United States: a modern country describing itself in Rome’s language.

title: Integration: How We Know About Rome
objective: After this level you can explain how historians use texts, inscriptions, coins and archaeology to study Rome.
summary: Ancient writers had biases, so historians test them against inscriptions, coins, letters and the archaeology of places like Pompeii.

cards.headline: A history of Rome is a detective story built from four kinds of clues.
cards.body: Texts, inscriptions, coins and the ground itself. Each clue tells part of the truth. None tells all of it.

cards.headline: Texts and their biases
cards.body: The obvious clue is the written word. Much of Roman history comes from ancient writers such as Livy, Tacitus and Suetonius. But each had his own sources, purposes and biases. Most accounts of Caligula come from later writers hostile to him, so historians treat the wildest stories with caution. And Rome’s founding stories were written down centuries after the events. Picture a witness who wasn’t there, and one who didn’t like the suspect.

cards.headline: Stone, metal and earth
cards.body: So historians check the writers against other clues. Huge numbers of Latin inscriptions carved in stone record laws, careers, dedications and epitaphs. Coins help date events and show how emperors wanted to be seen: each one a tiny press release in your pocket. Archaeology reveals the ordinary lives writers ignored, from houses and graves to rubbish heaps. Yes, Roman trash counts as evidence.

cards.fact: Ordinary Romans speak through the ground.
cards.context: Pompeii gives historians a rare snapshot of ordinary Roman town life. At Vindolanda, a fort near Hadrian’s Wall, archaeologists found more than a thousand wooden writing tablets, including a birthday invitation from one commander’s wife to another. The writers ignored lives like these. The ground kept them anyway.

cards.headline: The thread through it all
cards.body: Now the pattern. Again and again, whoever controlled the army controlled the state. After Marius, soldiers looked to their general, not the Senate, for pay and for land when they retired. So their loyalty followed the paymaster. Sulla marched his army on Rome. Caesar crossed the Rubicon with his. Vespasian, a general, won a civil war and a throne. In Rome, the road to power ran through the camp.
